title: Self-dressing clothes could help older adults
summary: KAIST and Stanford researchers built soft robotic tubes into fabric that use air pressure to guide clothing into place in about 10 seconds flat.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Most of us get dressed every day without thinking twice about it. However, a stiff shoulder can make pulling on a shirt surprisingly difficult, while balance problems can turn a simple pair of pants into a real challenge. That is what makes a new invention from South Korea's KAIST and Stanford University worth watching.

Researchers have created self-dressing clothes with soft, air-powered robots built into the fabric. Once activated, the garment moves along the body and helps guide itself into place, even while the wearer moves. The technology remains an early research project, but it shows how future clothing could help older adults get dressed with less assistance and stay independent at home longer.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL
The self-dressing system uses soft, air-powered robots to guide sleeves, a jacket and pants into place around the body. (KAIST)
How self-dressing clothes could support independence

Getting dressed ranks among the basic activities that often determine whether someone can live independently. When mobility or dexterity declines, people may need a spouse, family member or professional caregiver to help with a deeply personal routine.

The researchers behind the project say dressing challenges can reduce autonomy and increase reliance on caregivers. They designed the system for people with limited mobility, including older adults and those recovering from injuries. Stanford researchers have also identified dressing assistance as an important use for future home robots. The university says assistive technology could help older adults remain in their homes as caregiving needs increase.
Why dressing can become physically difficult

Dressing requires more movement than many people realize. You need to reach behind your body, lift your arms and shift your weight while handling fabric. Arthritis may make gripping or pulling clothing painful. Meanwhile, shoulder problems can limit your reach. Recovery from hip or knee surgery can also make bending difficult.

Balance adds another concern. Pulling on pants often requires someone to stand briefly on one leg or bend toward the floor. For a person who already feels unsteady, that familiar routine can become stressful. Self-dressing clothes could eventually reduce some of that reaching and pulling. However, researchers still need clinical studies to learn how well the system works for people with real mobility limitations.
How KAIST and Stanford's robotic clothing works

The researchers call their system SWAG, which stands for Self-Wearing Adaptive Garment. Instead of placing a large robotic arm next to the person, the team built flexible robotic tubes into the clothing. Air pressure causes these soft structures to unfold and grow along the body.

The movement turns the garment inside out as it advances. That approach allows the clothing to follow the person's shape while reducing friction between the fabric and skin. Think of ivy growing around a wall or tree. The plant advances from its tip rather than dragging its entire length forward. The soft robot uses a similar motion, which helps it follow curves and move across different surfaces.
In this demonstration, the robotic garment unfurls over the legs while the wearer remains seated. (KAIST)
A rainy bike ride sparked the robotic clothing idea
The idea began when KAIST postdoctoral researcher Nam Gyun Kim was riding his bike when it began to rain. As he kept moving, he wondered how helpful it would be if a raincoat could put itself on.

That simple idea led to a much bigger thought. Instead of making your body do all the pulling, reaching and twisting, what if the clothing could move into place on its own? From there, Kim and the research team began developing garments that use soft robotics to help dress the person wearing them.
How fast self-dressing clothes can work

Kim says putting on a full suit takes about 10 seconds. The published paper provides additional timing from individual demonstrations. A jacket moved into place in about 13 seconds, while the pants demonstration took roughly 21 seconds. A sleeve prototype took about 14 seconds.

The researchers tested sleeves, jackets and pants. Their results showed that the garments could unfold along the body while keeping contact forces within the team's safety limits. The system also relies on its physical design instead of a complicated control program. That could eventually help simplify the hardware needed for dressing assistance.
Why soft robotic clothing could feel more natural

Many existing dressing robots use rigid mechanical arms. Those systems must handle loose fabric while carefully avoiding uncomfortable contact with the person. They may also require the person to hold a fixed pose while the robot completes the task. That setup could feel awkward inside a bedroom or bathroom.

The KAIST and Stanford design takes a different approach by placing the robotic mechanism inside the garment. The clothing becomes the helper. Because the system uses soft materials, it can bend around the body rather than approaching it with a hard mechanical structure. KAIST says this design reduces physical strain and supports safer contact.
COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?
Flexible robotic tubes built into the jacket help pull the sleeves and fabric into position with less effort from the wearer. (KAIST)
Where self-dressing clothes could be used first

Older adults and people with disabilities represent a major potential use for the technology. KAIST also sees possibilities for rehabilitation patients who need temporary assistance after an injury or medical procedure. However, industrial workplaces may adopt the idea sooner.

Semiconductor employees frequently put on protective cleanroom clothing. Emergency workers may also need to suit up quickly while carrying other equipment. The researchers believe air-powered garments could help people put on protective clothing without relying heavily on their hands. The published study also discusses possible medical uses, such as helping healthcare workers apply protective coverings or compression bandages. Those applications remain potential future directions.
What self-dressing clothes still need to prove

The current system remains a research prototype connected to a pneumatic base station. Researchers have yet to announce a consumer price or release date. Several everyday questions remain unanswered. The garments would need to fit different body shapes and movement patterns. Designers would also need to address washing, storage and portable air power.

The research team says future versions may use adjustable sheaths or elastic materials to fit a wider range of bodies. The researchers also want to automate the garment-loading process and improve the controls.

Most importantly, the team says clinical trials involving people with mobility impairments will be essential. Those tests could show whether the clothing feels comfortable and works reliably outside the lab. Researchers also need to explore how the garment comes off. The current work concentrates mainly on dressing, while automated removal remains a future possibility.
What this means to you

You probably will not find robotic clothing hanging in a local store anytime soon. Yet this research gives us a useful preview of where assistive technology may be heading. For you or someone you care about, the biggest benefit could be control over a private daily routine. Clothing that handles part of the pulling and positioning could make mornings less tiring.
It could also delay the point when someone needs another person present simply to get dressed. That possibility still depends on testing, affordability and a design people feel comfortable wearing.
Kurt's key takeaways

Self-dressing clothes may sound unusual, but the need behind them is easy to understand. Arthritis, limited mobility or recovery from surgery can make getting dressed frustrating and exhausting. For older adults, a garment that helps guide itself into place could mean more privacy, less reliance on a caregiver and more confidence starting the day. The KAIST and Stanford system still has a long way to go. Researchers need to make it portable, test it with people who have mobility challenges and prove it can work safely in a home. Even so, the idea shows how technology could support independence through something as familiar as the clothes you already wear.

title: ClickLock Mac malware locks apps until you give in
summary: ClickLock Mac malware uses a fake verification page to trick users into pasting a Terminal command, then steals passwords and cryptocurrency wallets.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A routine "verify you are human" page should never ask you to open Terminal, the Mac app used to run computer commands. Yet that is how a new malware attack appears to get onto a Mac. The page tells you to copy and paste a command into Terminal. It then shows a convincing progress bar while the command quietly downloads malicious software in the background.

Next, a password box may appear that looks like a normal macOS request. If you cancel it, the malware can come back after you sign in again and repeatedly close Finder, your browser and other apps. Your Mac may feel almost impossible to use until you enter your login password.

The malware, called ClickLock, is built to steal personal information from your Mac. It searches for saved passwords, browser data and cryptocurrency wallet files. It can also install a hidden tool that lets an attacker reconnect to your computer later and control it remotely.

Researchers at cybersecurity company Group-IB discovered the malicious script on VirusTotal, an online service that checks files for threats. Someone first uploaded it there on June 9, 2026, yet none of the security tools on the platform detected it at the time of the researchers' report. Group-IB says the campaign has targeted at least 100 systems across 33 countries since May.
Here is how ClickLock takes over a Mac and what you can do to protect yourself.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
ClickLock may begin with a fake verification page that tells you to paste a command into Terminal. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What is ClickLock Mac malware?

ClickLock is a set of malicious scripts designed to steal sensitive information from a Mac. The malware can collect your Mac login password and browser data. It also searches for cryptocurrency wallet files, password manager extensions and information stored in macOS Keychain.
One component installs a persistent backdoor. That hidden connection can allow an attacker to access your Mac remotely even after the other parts of ClickLock remove themselves.
ClickLock gets started without exploiting a known macOS flaw. It also does not need admin-level access at the beginning. Instead, the attack depends on convincing you to run the command yourself.
How a fake verification starts the attack

Group-IB believes ClickLock likely spreads through a tactic called ClickFix. ClickFix attacks show you a fake error or verification request. The page then gives you a command that supposedly fixes the problem.

In this case, the ClickLock script displays a fake Cloudflare verification sequence after you paste the command into Terminal. An animated progress bar cycles through reassuring messages about checking browser signals and confirming you are human.

Meanwhile, the script disables keyboard interruptions and hides the Terminal cursor. It then downloads several malicious components in the background. Researchers have yet to confirm the exact landing pages used in the campaign. They also do not know whether people reached them through malicious search results, compromised websites, phishing messages or social media. However, the script's design strongly points to a ClickFix-style lure.
The password trap starts with a convincing pop-up

After the malware begins running, it displays a fake macOS password window. The pop-up uses your real username and an Apple icon downloaded by the attacker. If you enter a password, ClickLock checks it against your Mac. When the password works, the malware records it and sends it to the attacker through Telegram.

An incorrect password brings up another request. If you cancel the window, ClickLock installs two LaunchAgents. A LaunchAgent is a macOS instruction that can automatically run software when you sign in. In this case, the LaunchAgents bring the password-stealing components back at your next login.
HALLUSQUATTING AI ATTACK COULD HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER
The malware can repeatedly close apps and pressure you to enter your Mac login password. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
ClickLock can make your Mac feel unusable

When the password-stealing module returns, it begins closing visible apps every 210 milliseconds. It targets Finder, the Dock and Terminal. It also shuts down Activity Monitor, System Settings, Spotlight and common web browsers.

The fake password window may remain as the only useful item on your screen. That can make your Mac look broken while pressuring you to enter your password. Group-IB found that the loop can run for about 83 hours. It stops earlier when the malware captures a valid password.
A real Keychain prompt makes the attack more convincing

A second ClickLock component targets Chrome's Safe Storage key. Chromium-based browsers use this key to help encrypt passwords, cookies and autofill information stored on your Mac. An attacker with the key and copied browser databases may be able to decrypt that information offline.

This part of the attack triggers a genuine macOS Keychain authorization prompt. However, the malware caused the request. ClickLock then runs another process-closing loop while waiting for you to approve access. Researchers found that this loop repeats every 200 milliseconds and can continue for nearly 35 days. The script also suppresses macOS NotificationCenter for roughly six hours. That could hide warnings or notifications that might reveal the attack.
What ClickLock can steal from your Mac
ClickLock searches for information across eight browsers. Those browsers include Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Vivaldi, Arc and Chromium.
The targeted browser information includes:
Saved usernames and passwordsCookies and active session dataAutofill informationBookmarks and browser storageCryptocurrency wallet extensionsPassword manager extension data
Saved usernames and passwords
Cookies and active session data
Autofill information
Bookmarks and browser storage
Cryptocurrency wallet extensions
Password manager extension data

The malware also searches for desktop cryptocurrency wallets and encrypted wallet vaults. It can collect cached blockchain addresses across several networks. Other targets include macOS Keychain, Terminal command histories and FileZilla server details. The malware also records basic information about your Mac and its public IP address. ClickLock packages the collected information into a ZIP archive. It uploads that archive through Telegram's Bot API. Files larger than 40 MB get divided into smaller pieces, while retry code keeps trying after network failures.
If your Mac starts acting this way, shut it down and restart in Safe Mode before entering any password. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
ClickLock can leave a backdoor behind

One ClickLock component uses a modified version of the open-source GSocket tool. The malware installs a reverse shell, which gives the attacker a command-line connection to your Mac. On macOS, it disguises the backdoor as an iCloud-related process.

ClickLock uses a LaunchAgent and scheduled commands to keep the backdoor running. It also changes shell configuration files. Most of the other ClickLock modules delete themselves after completing their work. The GSocket component remains installed, which means the attacker may retain access after your Mac appears to return to normal.
Why ClickLock may be difficult to detect

The original ClickLock script had zero detections on VirusTotal when Group-IB analyzed it. Security vendors may update their detection tools as they learn more about the threat. The attackers also stored payloads on compromised websites that previously had clean reputations. Some components run without saving a normal file to the drive. Others erase themselves after stealing data.

However, ClickLock still produces suspicious activity while it runs. Warning signs include nonstop app closures, repeated password requests and sudden access to multiple browser folders. Security tools may also detect unusual connections to Telegram's API. For you, the earliest warning sign is much simpler. A website tells you to paste a command into Terminal. Legitimate human verification happens inside your browser. It should never require you to run a Terminal command.
Ways to stay safe from ClickLock Mac malware
These steps can help you avoid the ClickLock trap and respond quickly if the password loop starts.

Leave the page when it tells you to open Terminal and paste a command. A polished design offers no proof that the request is safe. Familiar logos can also be copied. Group-IB warns that a website asking you to use Terminal for verification is attempting to compromise your system.
Terminal commands can download software and change important settings. Never run an unfamiliar command simply to see what happens. Ask a trusted technical professional to inspect it first.

Think about what you were doing when the password window appeared. A website verification should have no reason to ask for your Mac login password. It should also have no reason to request access to Chrome information stored in Keychain. Cancel the request when the timing feels wrong.

Install macOS updates and keep automatic security updates turned on. Apple builds malware protection into macOS through Gatekeeper, Notarization and XProtect. Apple updates XProtect automatically as it identifies new malware. However, no built-in protection can eliminate every risk when you manually run a malicious command.

Strong antivirus software can provide another layer of protection against malicious files and suspicious behavior. Still, a clean scan cannot guarantee that ClickLock left nothing behind. The backdoor persists after other components erase themselves. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Do not enter your password to make the pop-up disappear. Press and hold your Mac's power button for up to 10 seconds until the computer shuts down. On a MacBook with Touch ID, press and hold the Touch ID button. Group-IB recommends forcing a shutdown when your Mac becomes unresponsive and keeps requesting your password. The company then recommends starting the Mac in Safe Mode.

Mac with Apple silicon: Wait until the Mac shuts down completely. Press and hold the power button until "Loading startup options" appears. Select your startup volume. Hold the Shift key, then click Continue in Safe Mode.
Intel-based Mac: Turn on or restart the Mac. Immediately press and hold the Shift key until the login window appears.

Once Safe Mode starts, turn off Wi-Fi or unplug the Ethernet cable. Then contact Apple Support or a trusted cybersecurity professional. Removing a browser extension or clearing your history will not remove ClickLock's persistent backdoor.

Use a separate trusted device to change the password for your primary email account. Then secure your Apple Account and any financial accounts stored on the Mac. Change password manager credentials and review active sessions. Sign out of devices or sessions you do not recognize. Review the devices connected to your Apple Account and remove unfamiliar ones. Apple also recommends changing your Apple Account password when you suspect unauthorized access. After a professional cleans or resets the Mac, change its local login password. Assume the attacker received that password if you entered it into the ClickLock window.
Kurt's key takeaways

ClickLock depends on one dangerous moment: convincing you to paste a command into Terminal. Once that happens, the malware can begin stealing information before the password pressure even starts. The biggest red flag is easy to remember. No trustworthy website needs Terminal to prove you are human. If your Mac starts closing apps and demanding a password, shut it down rather than giving in. Start in Safe Mode and get help checking for the persistent backdoor. Then use another trusted device to secure your most important accounts.

title: Florida mail carrier accused of snatching pets on route, trapping 100-plus cats and dogs in ‘hoarding’ house
summary: A Florida mail carrier allegedly kept more than 100 animals in feces-filled cages with no air conditioning, and now owners are lining up for pet reunions.
story: Bodycam video shows investigators responding to a Florida home where they rescued more than 100 animals from what police said were "deplorable" conditions in a woman’s home. (Martin County Sheriff’s Office)
The "worst animal hoarding case" a Florida sheriff has ever seen is now expanding as more animals are being recovered.
Some of the rescued animals already have been reunited with owners who said they’d given up hope of ever seeing them again.

Gail Giustino, a 77-year-old mail carrier, was arrested July 20 after authorities found more than 100 animals held in feces-filled cages in her Stuart home. She’d been "collecting cats" she found along her mail route, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said.
Gail Giustino, 77, has been charged with one count of animal cruelty and one count of confinement of animals without sufficient exercise. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)
RIDGLAN FARMS RESCUE BEAGLES FIND NEW LIFE HELPING VETERANS OVERCOME WAR TRAUMA WITH PAWS OF WAR

With no air conditioning or ventilation, the home was "probably 110 degrees" on the late July day when the animals were removed, Budensiek said in a news conference on July 20 outside Giustino’s home.

"We were coming out here thinking maybe 15, 20, 30 cats," he told reporters, as people wearing white hazmat suits carried out cages holding dozens of cats and at least a dozen small dogs. There was "a foot of animal feces" in parts of the house, Budensiek said.

Some of the caged cats were held fast in feces that had hardened like concrete. Staffers had to smash bricks of feces from around the cats’ legs to allow them to move, Sarah Fisher, spokeswoman for the Humane Society of Treasure Coast, told Fox News Digital.

"When we cracked the door…the stench was unreal," Budensiek said. "The air was stifling hot." He went on to say, "She never walks the pets. She never brings them outside of the house. They've been confined to that animal jail really for however long she's been hoarding these pets."
Investigators recovered animals from inside the home of Gail Giustino in Stuart, Fla., on July 20, 2026. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)
PARTNER OF WOMAN KILLED BY DOGS RECENTLY SAVED NEIGHBOR WOUNDED IN SIMILAR ATTACK: COURT RECORDS

Investigators faced an "overwhelming" smell of "animal urine, feces, and ammonia," an odor that wafted outside the house, authorities said. The "deplorable" conditions inside the house left "no safe path of entry due to excessive debris, animal feces, and urine," investigators reported.
The odor inside the residence was so severe that it "presented a potential health hazard to responding personnel," arrest records show.
Since 2014, local animal control had issued "up to 65 civil citations" to Giustino for the conditions she’s kept animals, the sheriff said.
DOG SAVED FROM ISIS BY ARMY VETERAN 'KIDNAPPED' FROM FAMILY YARD BY LOCAL AUTHORITIES

And code enforcement officers helped her add air-conditioning units, Budensiek said. But investigators found that those units were not working. And "we haven’t been out here checking on her for the last 10 years," he said.

Giustino could have been charged with up to 160 counts of animal cruelty, Budensiek said. Instead, she was charged with one misdemeanor count of animal cruelty and one misdemeanor count of confinement of animals without sufficient exercise. She was released on a $50,000 bond.
"We truly believe that Gail thinks she's doing the right thing," he said. "But she's doing it the wrong way."
Investigators recovered dogs and cats from inside the house of Gail Giustino in Stuart, Fla., on July 20, 2026. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)
He said, "The goal of arresting her was to be able to seize the animals, to save them from death and try to get them the help that they need."
They also hoped the process would lead to mental health treatment for Giustino, he said. She did not respond to a request for comment by Fox News Digital.
Giustino started working for the U.S. Postal Service in 1997 and is still employed, said Debra Jean Fetterly, a USPS spokesperson for South Florida.
"We are aware of the situation," Fetterly told Fox News Digital. "The Postal Service does not publicly discuss personnel matters."
‘They know they’re safe’
Days after the arrest, Martin County officials were able to trap and bring in three of four cats that escaped during the rescue effort at Giustino’s home.
And a friend surrendered five more small dogs Giustino allegedly left in her care, Fisher said. By July 29, the humane society had received 108 animals from Giustino’s home.
"We unfortunately are anticipating more of Gail's animals to be coming in the coming weeks" from her friends’ homes, Fisher said. "The sheriff's looking into that right now."
"We don't know really what to expect, but we're prepared."
Meanwhile, staffers have struggled emotionally, she said, because the animals "were in pretty terrible shape."
Two dogs removed from the home of Gail Giustino receive care at the Humane Society of Treasure Coast. (Courtesy of Sarah Fisher)
"They were really just shut down. Some of the cats were catatonic; they wouldn't even move. They were traumatized."
But now, they’ve started showing signs of healing.

"It's actually filling our hearts right now because they have been coming out of their shells," Fisher said. "These cats that weren’t even lifting their heads up are now meowing and seeking attention, and I think they know they're safe."
The 12 tiny dogs recovered from Giustino’s home showed signs of improvement faster, she said.

They were thin, flea-covered, missing hair because of neglect, and were suffering with dental disease, Fisher said. They range in age from 2 to 8, she said, and many appear to be Yorkshire terriers, also known as Yorkies.
"Dogs are just different," Fisher said. "They were happy as could be. They knew they were saved and they were happy. … It's really giving us hope at the shelter."
Further bolstering spirits is the enthusiastic support from locals, Fisher said.
They’ve flooded the shelter with requests to adopt the neglected animals. They’ve brought pizzas, pastries and other treats for workers.
"It’s been beautiful to see," she said.
A big part of the project involves trying to arrange for reunions with potential owners.
On Friday morning, July 24, hearts overflowed with hope outside the shelter.
Dozens of people from all walks of life queued up in the blazing Florida heat, all waiting to see if their missing pets were among those rescued.
Jisel Leon reunites with her cat, Blizzard, at the Humane Society of Treasure Coast in Palm City, Fla., on July 24, 2026. (Courtesy of Sarah Fisher)
"We had 50-plus people, very, very eager right when the doors opened at 10 o’clock," she said.
"They were very wonderful and patient. And one by one, they were all walking out crying because their animals weren't with us."
Shelter employees had hoped for joyful reunions.
"There were grown men crying; there were kids crying. It was so emotional," Fisher said. "It was really, really hard."
By the end of that Friday, two more pet owners rejoiced over their unexpected reunions.
And staffers hope there will be more in the coming days as word spreads about the recovered animals, she said.
Any of the dogs and cats not claimed eventually will be available for adoption. There’s no timeline yet for that.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
"We want to make sure that any of these owned animals are going to be going home with their owners, and we're not accidentally going to be adopting them out."
Linh Nguyen called her reunion with 6-year-old Patchy a clear answer to prayer.
Linh Nguyen and Patchy walk by the water in Stuart, Fla., on July 24, 2026. (Courtesy of Linh Nguyen)
SEND US A TIP
He’d disappeared from her yard in early January.
"I’d been praying for his return for seven months," Nguyen told Fox News Digital.
GOT A TIP?
As she prayed, she said she told God she knew it was just "a little thing, just a cat."
But her faith told her that anything was possible.
She posted fliers offering a $5,000 reward for Patchy’s return. She rode her bike through the neighborhood late at night calling his name until she was hoarse. And she kept praying.
"If You do a miracle and bring my cat home," she pleaded in faith, "I will tell everyone it is You."

Then she saw a news report about the rescued cats. She had a strong feeling her missing pet might be among them. And when she stepped into the Humane Society, he saw her right away, she said. She heard meowing that got progressively louder.
"I couldn’t see him, but I recognized his voice."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Now, Nguyen said, Patchy is thriving at home again and is enjoying walks on a leash.

She’s relieved to know that others are being reunited with their pets, she said. And she’s glad to know that Giustino "will get the help that she needs."
"This," Nguyen said, "is a pure miracle."

title: Savannah Guthrie makes desperate plea six months after mom Nancy went missing: 'Someone knows something'
summary: Savannah Guthrie's desperate plea reveals her family's six-month agony as Pima County releases ransom notes demanding $4 million in bitcoin.
story: Forensics and missing persons expert Sheryl McCollum analyzes the release of alleged ransom notes sent to Nancy Guthrie’s family on ‘Fox News @ Night.’
NBC "TODAY" co-host Savannah Guthrie made a desperate plea for the public's help in a Saturday morning social media post, exactly six months since her mother Nancy was reported missing.

"This is our beautiful Mom. Six months ago, someone took her out of her bed in the dead of night. We have lived every moment, every breath, and every heartbeat in agony and despair ever since," Guthrie wrote to open her Instagram message.

"Every day, we wake up and try to be strong and go on - because that’s what our joyful and resilient Mom taught us to do," she continued. "But make no mistake - our hearts are in ruins. Cam and Kristine, Annie and Tommy, Mike and me - we spend every waking moment thinking of her, longing for her, looking for her."

"There is a hole inside us that can never be filled," Savannah wrote. "There is an ache that cannot be softened. And there is a determination in us that cannot be quenched - to find out what happened to her, so that we can give her the dignity of a proper goodbye - a celebration of her remarkable life that she so deserves."
NEW DETAILS FROM NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM DEMAND REVEALED, 'HER LIFE IS IN YOUR HANDS': REPORT
A photo of Nancy Guthrie that Savannah Guthrie posted to Instagram on Aug. 1, 2026, on the six-month anniversary of her mother's disappearance. (Savannah Guthrie/ Instagram)

Guthrie's early morning post came just one day after the Pima County Sheriff's Department released a pair of ransom notes Friday in the hopes that someone might recognize the documents' "unique linguistic style."

"We are begging for help. We are desperate," Savannah's post continued. "We need someone to come forward. Someone knows something. Someone suspects something. Someone recognizes the writing in the ransom demand notes."

"Someone has noticed something different, strange, troubling or just unusual - perhaps with someone they deeply love," she wrote. "Perhaps they are afraid to come forward. Perhaps they are conflicted. Perhaps they are angry or upset for being in this situation. There is a way out - to tell what you know. You can do so anonymously. The reward is available. There is a way to end this situation and do the right thing."
Savannah Guthrie poses alongside her mother Nancy Guthrie during a production break whilst hosting NBC's "TODAY" live from Australia. (Don Arnold/WireImage)

"We are real people, facing real grief, doing the best we can, and counting our many blessings along the way - most especially the prayers and love from good people, which we feel deeply. We need your prayers, we need your kindness. We need the good to be stronger than the evil. If you are following this story for entertainment or for profit, you are not on her side - you are part of the harm perpetrated against her. We will never stop looking for answers - and we will never stop looking for the light. We will always be hoping and praying and believing in the best of our world - in spite of circumstance. This is what our faith makes possible. Please. Bring her home," she concluded.
NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTES DON'T MATCH SUSPECT'S BEHAVIOR, PROFILER SAYS: 'I DON'T BELIEVE THEY'RE REAL'
The 84-year-old Nancy Guthrie was last seen outside her home in the Catalina Hills near Tucson, Arizona, on Jan. 31.
The home's doorbell camera recorded a masked intruder disconnecting the cameras at approximately 1:47 a.m. local time on Feb. 1.
An undated photo of Nancy Guthrie and Savannah Guthrie provided by NBC in repsonse to the disappearance of the 84 year-old mother of the "TODAY" host. (Courtesy of NBC)
At 2:28 a.m., her pacemaker lost its Bluetooth connection to her cell phone, according to the Pima County Sheriff's Department.

The newly released ransom notes, which the sheriff's department said were sent on Feb. 2 and Feb. 6, demanded a ransom of $4 million to be paid in Bitcoin, while the author threatened to kill Nancy Guthrie.

The notes included references to the crime scene that may not have been public at the time they were sent — including details about the location of Guthrie's Apple Watch and the smashed floodlight in her backyard. Fox News Digital first learned about the watch on the morning of Tuesday, Feb. 3. According to authorities, the note had been sent the day before, on Monday, Feb. 2, indicating the sender knew about it before the information began to seep out into the public sphere.
NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTE CLAIMED THAT SHE HAD DIED, BEEN ‘BURIED WITH NATURE,’ SOURCE SAYS
The second note claimed that Nancy Guthrie had "perished."
Fox News Digital contacted the Pima County Sheriff's Department for further comment.

title: Bryan Kohberger's choice of 'a house full of women' may hold the key to the Idaho murders' biggest mystery
summary: The Netflix docuseries "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare" explores whether Bryan Kohberger's struggles with women fueled the deadly attack.
story: A judge approved Bryan Kohberger's request for a new lawyer in his attempt to secure a new trial, despite his previous guilty plea for murdering four University of Idaho students in 2022. Bryan Kohberger took the motive for the Idaho murders to his prison cell. One filmmaker believes the answer may lie in why he chose the house he attacked.

"The fact that [this] was the house that he chose. This was a house that had five women living in it. The night that the murders happened, Xana Kernodle’s boyfriend, Ethan Chapin, was over, but really, this was a house full of women, and it seems quite clear that he targeted it," Skye Borgman, director of the Netflix docuseries "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare," told Fox News Digital.

title: Weapons stockpile shortages impacting military strategy in the Mideast
summary: U.S. missile interceptor stockpiles are shrinking, raising readiness concerns.
story: Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin has the latest on the U.S. weapons stockpile amid the Iran war on 'America Reports.'
The Pentagon is confronting a growing reality after months of fighting Iran: America's stockpile of missile defense interceptors.
It is shrinking so much, military planners are weighing whether they can continue the current cycle of limited retaliatory strikes.

The Center for Strategic and International Studies, using open-source budget numbers provided to Congress, estimates U.S. Patriot interceptor inventories have fallen from roughly 2,300 pre-war to fewer than 827.
THAAD interceptor inventories have also dropped from 452 to fewer than 278.
A Patriot missile is launched from a desert site during the annual U.S.-Israeli Juniper Cobra air defense exercise in southern Israel. (Photo by IDF via Getty Images)
CSIS warns rebuilding those stockpiles could take three years or more, raising concerns about protecting U.S. forces and bases worldwide if another major conflict erupts, for instance in the Pacific.

"If you look at what we've expended for the Patriots, for example, over half the global inventory has now been consumed in the Middle East. Similar to the THAAD interceptors as well," said Kelly Grieco, a missile expert at the Stimson Center.

"These are things that we have to intercept ballistic missiles. Almost half of THAAD interceptors have been used. So that's global inventory. So that really leaves us with very little excess to be able to use in other theaters, whether it's defending US forces in Europe or the Indo-Pacific. So this becomes quite a constraint, I would say, on the United States capabilities, not just today, but in the years to come."

The Pentagon’s $67 billion request for fiscal year 2026 emergency funding includes $18.2 billion to replace the U.S.’s most advanced Patriot missile, Navy Tomahawks and the Army’s high-altitude interceptor known as THAAD, according to Bloomberg.
Half of the munitions requested in the Pentagon's 2027 budget are low-cost munitions worth $600,000 or less.
US NAVY PLANS MAJOR TORPEDO STOCKPILE OVERHAUL AS MILITARY SHIFTS TO TWO-WAR STRATEGY
By 2031, 70 percent of the munitions purchased by the Pentagon are expected to be in this lower-cost range, according to Jerry McGinn, who tracks the defense industrial base at CSIS.

"The munitions we use today are incredibly effective: the Tomahawk, the Patriot, the theater missile defense interceptors, or THAAD, that you've seen in the press are incredibly effective. They were built solely for performance, and they were designed a long time ago," McGinn said.

"They weren't built or designed to be produced at scale. So they take two to three years from this contract award to actually come off the assembly line because these are very intricate systems. They're essentially handmade in a lot of ways. So it's hard to scale production on these efforts."
Pentagon building in Washington. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)
Operation Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury burned through numerous missiles, but concerns about stockpiles preceded the latest Middle East conflict.

McGinn and others described a recent Pentagon meeting in which the department summoned a dozen leading Silicon Valley defense firms such as Shield AI and Anduril to discuss urgently replenishing depleted U.S. weapons inventories as the war consumes precision munitions.

"Concerns are that these companies have not produced at scale," McGinn added. "They have commercial kinds of technologies. They've done prototyping, but are they able to have production lines that can work with the government to produce those munitions at scale?"
Brandon Tseng attended the Pentagon meeting.
This former Navy SEAL started SHIELD AI over a decade ago at a time when Silicon Valley did not want to partner with the Pentagon, and it was hard to get venture capital money.
Just two years ago, 10,000 defense tech startups were formed.

"Defense tech was not a word in 2015. Venture capitalists thought we were crazy. When we said we wanted to work on this mission of protecting service members and civilians, they just didn't believe you could build a business behind it," Tseng told Fox.
He was recently in Ukraine where his V-BAT, an AI-driven targeting system, is being used to strike Russian targets.

"It's a miniature Predator or Reaper drone. It does the mission of these $40 million aircraft at a fraction of the price — roughly a million dollars per aircraft," Tseng explained how Ukraine is using the cheaper version for "intelligence surveillance, reconnaissance and targeting" at very long ranges.
The V-BAT "can operate when GPS or communications are jammed because it has our AI pilot Hivemind on board," Tseng said.
TRUMP DECLARES HAMAS TO DISARM AS SAUDI MILITARY READIES FOR POTENTIAL HOUTHI GROUND OFFENSIVE

story: Fox News correspondent Steve Harrigan reports on the Alex Murdaugh double murder retrial kicking off in Lexington, South Carolina. story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A small town in Colorado has been declared abandoned by the state after its remaining elected officials resigned, leading its troubled water system to become a "health hazard" to its residents, according to state officials.

The Office of the Colorado Secretary of State said the determination was made this week after a public hearing showed that "the Town of Hartman had no Board of Trustees or Town Clerk, was unable to hold a town election, and owned infrastructure critical for the treatment or delivery of water to residents."

"Importantly, not determining that the Town of Hartman is abandoned as contemplated by § 31-3-201(1)(b), C.R.S. (2026), would leave the residents in further legal limbo during a health hazard, with no authority to conduct business, hold elections, or fix their water infrastructure so that clean water can be delivered to the town residents," Deputy Secretary of State Andrew Kline wrote in an abandonment order. "Abandonment is the only legal mechanism in Colorado statute that creates an avenue for residents of the area to receive clean water."
DISNEYLAND GUESTS LEFT SCRAMBLING AFTER WATER OUTAGE SHUTS BATHROOMS AND RESTAURANTS
The town of Hartman, Colo., on Thursday, Feb. 26, 2026. (Denver Post via Getty Images)

Hartman, which has a population of 30 in southeast Colorado, saw its three active trustees resign in January, a day after a brawl erupted between four women following a board of trustees meeting, according to The Denver Post.

"Our safety was more important than having a government," Pam Packer, one of the trustees who resigned, told the newspaper, which also reported that the mayor resigned in October and that Hartman previously was grappling with embezzlement allegations and restraining orders.

Kline said in the abandonment order that in mid-June, "Ms. Jessie Simmons, a self-attested resident, landowner, and elector of the Town of Hartman, submitted a written application to the Secretary of State for determination of abandonment for the Town of Hartman alleging that the town does not have a board of trustees or town clerk, is unable to hold an election, and owns and operates water infrastructure needed to treat and deliver water to residents."

"Ms. Simmons further asserted that as of time of her application, the Town of Hartman had lacked chlorine in its water for over one month and the water was not potable and 'smells horrible.’ She stated that the Town of Hartman had been under an order to boil water for months," he wrote.
EXPERTS REVEAL HOW TO AVOID DEADLY LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE AS NYC OUTBREAK KILLS 5
Former Hartman board member Velma Cooper and her husband, Mark, sit at their house in Hartman, Colo., on Thursday, Feb. 26, 2026. (Denver Post via Getty Images)

At a hearing on July 13, Eric Bergman, the director of the Division of Local Government for the Department of Local Affairs, "testified that he has regional managers throughout the state, and one in Southeast Colorado that has worked extensively with the Town of Hartman for the last 5 or 6 years," according to Kline.

"Mr. Bergman also testified that since 2022, DOLA representatives have been in the Town of Hartman over 30 times helping with elections, turnover, recalls, resignations, budgets, audits, grant administration, and training of new officials. In January of 2026, DOLA received letters of resignation from each of the town's then-Trustees. Since the resignation of these elected officials, no government officials or government remain in the Town of Hartman," the order stated.

"There are no government officials in the Town of Hartman who are authorized to approve contracts, spend funds, appoint replacements, certify elections, or make decisions regarding the Town of Hartman's water system. Mr. Bergman testified there is also no clerk or governing body to call, conduct, or certify a municipal election," it continued.

"According to Mr. Bergman, the Town of Hartman is facing a public health threat. Mr. Bergman testified that the Town of Hartman has been on a boil advisory since last October 2025, and the water currently needs testing and chlorine. The water tank is compromised and needs repair or replacement," Kline also wrote in the order. "There is no one operating the water system at this time. DOLA, along with the Colorado Department of Health and Environment had previously provided grants for more than $1 million to the Town of Hartman to work on the water system. Those funds were reimbursement-based. However, without government officials, the Town is unable to enter any contracts that would enable it to access the grant funds."
Power lines line First Street in Hartman, Colo., on Thursday, Feb. 26, 2026. (Denver Post via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Office of Colorado’s Secretary of State said that, following the abandonment order, "All existing streets, avenues, and alleys previously located within the abandoned town that are not owned by a third party shall be vested in the Board of County Commissioners of Prowers County," and that "Ownership of water infrastructure critical for the treatment or delivery of water to residents shall be vested in Prowers County, which shall transfer said infrastructure to an entity whose primary purpose is water treatment or delivery."
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

The 35-year-old Ohio native was reportedly found shot "execution-style" with a gunshot wound to the back of his head while on a camping trip on Playa La Selva in Luquillo, Puerto Rico.
His body was found on July 10. Local outlet El Nuevo Dia reports police have a person of interest in Wilkin's case, on Thursday.

OHIO MAN FOUND SHOT DEAD IN EXECUTION-STYLE KILLING WHILE CAMPING ON PUERTO RICO BEACH: REPORTS

MICHIGAN ATHLETE LURED BY SNAPCHAT MESSAGE BEFORE BEING SHOT, DUMPED IN LAKE WHILE STILL ALIVE

title: ICE lodges detainer for illegal immigrant accused of trying to disarm Virginia police officer
summary: ICE lodged a detainer against a Honduran national who allegedly ambushed and tried to disarm a Fairfax County police officer in Annandale, Virginia.
story: Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino address the migrant crime surge in Virginia, as illegal immigrants face serious charges, including sexual offenses. Griff Jenkins reports on cases in Fairfax County, involving Israel Flores Ortiz and Angel David Rubio Moran. Josh Holmes critiques Governor Abigail Spanberger's executive order, which ended cooperation with ICE, exacerbating tensions over sanctuary policies and their impact on public safety in the commonwealth.
Federal immigration officials have lodged a detainer against a Honduran national accused of attempting to disarm a police officer during an encounter in Northern Virginia.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is asking Fairfax County officials not to release Nehemia Noel Fuentes-Banegas after authorities said he ambushed a Fairfax County police officer Tuesday.
According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), officers responded to a report of a man who left a home in Annandale following an argument while allegedly armed with two knives.
SPANBERGER'S ICE ROLLBACK TO BLAME FOR TODDLER KILLING, VIRGINIA 'HOTBED' OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRIME: DHS

A Fairfax County police officer's body camera captures the encounter with Nehemia Noel Fuentes-Banegas, who is accused of attempting to disarm the officer in Annandale, Virginia. (Fairfax County Police Department)
Fairfax County police said the man also stabbed himself before leaving the residence and fleeing into a nearby wooded area.
As officers searched a wooded area, Fuentes-Banegas allegedly emerged from the brush, grabbed an officer's firearm and attempted to disarm the officer, DHS said.
Fairfax County police said one officer fired his service weapon while a second officer simultaneously deployed a department-issued Taser. The bullet grazed Fuentes-Banegas' shoulder, police said.
Fuentes-Banegas was arrested and charged with attempted disarming of a law enforcement officer. ICE has lodged a detainer requesting that Fairfax County notify federal authorities before his release.
ILLEGAL ALIEN ‘MONSTER’ CHARGED WITH RAPING DEAD GIRLFRIEND’S DAUGHTER, DHS BLAMES BIDEN-ERA POLICIES

Nehemia Noel Fuentes-Banegas is accused of attempting to disarm a Fairfax County police officer during an encounter in Northern Virginia, according to authorities. Federal immigration officials have lodged a detainer seeking his transfer to ICE custody. (Fairfax County Police Department)
According to DHS, Fuentes-Banegas entered the United States illegally through Texas in 2022 and was later released under the Biden administration.
"This criminal illegal alien from Honduras attacked a law enforcement officer and attempted to take the officer's gun," DHS Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin said in a statement.

"He has now been charged with attempted disarming of a law enforcement officer," she continued. "ICE is calling on Governor Abigail Spanberger and her fellow sanctuary politicians to commit to not releasing this dangerous criminal from jail."
DHS blamed Virginia's sanctuary policies for limiting cooperation with federal immigration authorities, arguing they have made the commonwealth "a magnet for illegal alien crime."
ABIGAIL SPANBERGER’S VIRGINIA A ‘HOTBED’ FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRIME, DHS SAYS AFTER LATEST RAPE CHARGE

Two knives were recovered during the arrest of Nehemia Noel Fuentes-Banegas, who is accused of attempting to disarm a Fairfax County police officer in Annandale, Virginia. (Fairfax County Police Department)
The department noted that Spanberger signed executive orders at the start of her administration ending former Gov. Glenn Youngkin's 287(g) agreements and limiting state cooperation with ICE.
"Under Governor Spanberger, Virginia has become a hotbed of illegal alien crime," DHS said.

DHS also pointed to the recent arrest of Raul Genesis Ortiz Moran, a Mexican national charged with second-degree murder and aggravated sexual battery in connection with the death of a 2-year-old girl in Louisa County.

"This horrific tragedy was completely avoidable because this illegal alien should have never been in our country. Governor Spanberger’s sanctuary policies have made Virginia a hotbed for illegal alien crime," DHS Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis previously told Fox News Digital.

title: Mystery stranger vanishes after family says frantic warning saved their lives during devastating house fire
summary: The Las Vegas family is now searching for the unidentified hero they say woke them during a July 5 house fire they believe was caused by fireworks.
story: Surveillance video captures the unidentified passerby who alerted a sleeping family to a dangerous house fire before trying to help fight the flames. Credit: Danna Shabtai
A mysterious stranger is being hailed as a hero after waking a sleeping Las Vegas family, helping them escape a predawn house fire and then disappearing before anyone could learn his name.

The family is now searching for the man they say pounded on their front door, screamed "Fire!" and even grabbed a garden hose to battle the flames before quietly leaving, hoping to thank the person they believe saved not only their lives, but their neighbors' lives as well.
The fire broke out shortly before 5 a.m. on July 5 at the family's home in the Las Vegas Valley.
Home surveillance video shared with Fox News Digital shows flames engulfing the backyard as the fire spread.
BENNY JOHNSON RECALLS HOW CHARLIE KIRK HELPED HIS FAMILY AFTER ARSON DESTROYED THEIR DC HOME
Video shows the unidentified man who alerted a Las Vegas family to a house fire. (Danna Shabtai)

Speaking with Fox News Digital, homeowner Danna Shabtai said she had gone to bed after asking children across the street to stop setting off fireworks near her home on the night of July 4. Hours later, at 4:51 a.m., she woke to someone frantically ringing the doorbell and pounding on the front door.
"My dog started barking, so I woke up, and I stumbled to the door," Shabtai said. "I opened the door and the gentleman was yelling, 'Fire! Fire!'"
"He pointed toward the back of the house, and I turned around, and I could see the French doors to the backyard. I just saw orange — like a wall of orange."
ICE OFFICER HAILED AS HERO AFTER SAVING DRIVER INJURED IN MISSOURI CRASH
The unidentified man is seen on surveillance video moments before alerting a Las Vegas family to a dangerous house fire. (Danna Shabtai)

After realizing the fire was far more serious than she initially thought, Shabtai said her sister grabbed the family's garden hose and rushed outside to fight the flames while she scooped up her 14-month-old son and ran next door to wake her neighbors.
"I started banging on their windows and their door, trying to make noise, like, 'Wake up! Wake up!'" Shabtai said.
She said two women joined her in pounding on the neighbors' door until everyone inside made it out safely.
CRUISE PASSENGER HAILED AS HERO AFTER JUMPING INTO WATER TO SAVE 84-YEAR-OLD MAN
The family's backyard sustained extensive fire damage after a blaze erupted early July 5. The homeowners say an unidentified stranger woke them moments before the flames spread. (Danna Shabtai)
Meanwhile, the stranger grabbed a hose from the neighboring home and tried to keep the flames from spreading.

"He went to those neighbors' house and grabbed their hose from the front yard, and he was trying to put out their fire," Shabtai said. "So not only did he wake us up, he was trying to put out the fire with my sister."
Shabtai believes the man's actions prevented an even greater tragedy.
"If he wasn't driving by at that time, I don't know. It would have been a lot worse before we would have even noticed or woken up that there was a fire," she said.
The family has since taken to social media in hopes of identifying the mystery man so they can thank him in person.

"You're an angel. You saved our lives, and I'm really thankful for everything that you did," Shabtai previously told Fox 5 Las Vegas. "You didn't have to stop. You could have driven by and said, probably someone already called it in. But no, you took the time, and you woke us up, and you're a hero."
Extensive fire damage is visible in the backyard of a Las Vegas Valley home after flames spread between neighboring properties. (Danna Shabtai)
Speaking directly to the mystery man, Shabtai thanked him for stopping when others may have driven by.
"You saved probably two households and a bunch of pets because it would have been way too far gone before we would have realized," she said. "You saved our lives. You're a hero."
Shabtai said she believes the fire began after children across the street continued setting off fireworks despite being asked to stop.

She said she heard debris landing on a neighbor's gazebo and believes she saw a glowing ember drift over a roof toward the neighboring property before everyone went to bed. She believes the ember may have smoldered for hours before igniting the fire, though officials have not determined an official cause.
In a Facebook post after the fire, Shabtai credited the unidentified passerby with saving multiple families and expressed frustration over what she believes caused the blaze.

"This is why you leave fireworks to the professionals," she wrote. "This guy who just happened to drive by saved our lives and our neighbors' lives. Next year I'll be standing outside with my garden hose and hosing down any feral kids lighting up fireworks in my neighborhood."
She later shared a video of the aftermath, writing that while her family was fortunate to remain in its home, others were not.

"Aftermath of fire. Neighbors are displaced now because of fireworks. Luckily we don't have to leave," she wrote.
Fox News Digital reached out to the North Las Vegas Fire Department for additional information about the cause of the fire but did not immediately receive a response.

title: Nancy Guthrie update: DNA couldn't be profiled from crime scene hair sample, sheriff says
summary: DNA testing on a hair sample found in Nancy Guthrie's home returned no profile, but investigators say the sample may still prove valuable as the case continues.
story: Scientists weren't able to generate a DNA profile from a hair sample collected from Nancy Guthrie's home, Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos told Fox News Digital Thursday. But it still may be useful to investigators.

TUCSON, Ariz. — Investigators couldn't obtain a DNA profile from a hair sample recovered inside Nancy Guthrie’s home, Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos told Fox News Digital in a new interview Thursday as the case nears its six-month mark.
"Yes, there was a hair. We had it and thought, 'OK, well, we'll do the DNA first,' right? You're going to do DNA before something else," he explained.
Working with the FBI, investigators sent the sample to a California laboratory for additional DNA testing.
NANCY GUTHRIE'S SUSPECTED ABDUCTION: TIMELINE OF EVENTS IN DISAPPEARANCE OF 'TODAY' HOST'S MOM

This image released by the FBI shows an armed individual appearing to have tampered with the camera at Nancy Guthrie's front door the morning of her disappearance in Tucson, Ariz., Feb. 1, 2026. At right is an undated photo of Nancy Guthrie provided by NBC in response to the disappearance of the 84-year-old mother of "Today" show host Savannah Guthrie. (Provided by FBI; Courtesy of NBC)
"It came back ... there's no DNA," Nanos said. "But does that mean the hair isn't that of the suspect? We won't know that till we have the suspect's hair. You don't just destroy it."
Investigators have preserved the sample, and it still may be of use later, he added.
GOT A TIP?

This image released by the FBI shows an armed individual who appears to have a light emitting from his mouth at Nancy Guthrie's front door the morning of her disappearance in Tucson, Ariz., Feb. 1, 2026. (Provided by FBI)
"There's other things that hair may prove valuable for, but right now it was just about, 'Is there any DNA there?' And the answer was no," the sheriff said. "That was just a matter of weeks ago."
Guthrie is the 84-year-old mother of "Today" co-host Savannah Guthrie. She will have been missing for six months on Saturday.
Nanos indicated the hair was only one part of the broader DNA work underway, though he did not specify how many other samples are being tested.
DNA testing remains a priority in the case, and Nanos said investigators continue working with multiple crime labs to analyze evidence collected from the home.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
A tent was placed over the front entrance to Nancy Guthrie's home in Tucson, Ariz., Feb. 12, 2026. The tent covers where Guthrie's blood was found. (Fox Flight Team)
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
"Anything we can grasp onto with DNA is a part of this investigation," he said.
That includes investigative genetic genealogy research, which is used to generate leads from a family tree. He noted rapid advances in DNA technology.
NANCY GUTHRIE CASE COULD HINGE ON MYSTERY TIPSTER WHO EMAILED TMZ

Deputies examine a flyer taped to Nancy Guthrie's mailbox Feb. 22, 2026. They were called there after volunteer searchers and several streamers walked onto Guthrie's property with a shovel. (Michael Ruiz/Fox News Digital)
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
"That's really where some of my optimism is, that I just know that we're gonna get this thing resolved," Nanos said.
There is a combined reward of more than $1.2 million that remains unclaimed.
"We believe, just as the family does, just as Savannah does, somebody knows something. We need that person to call us."

Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos exits the press room after giving an update on the investigation into the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie, the 84-year-old mother of U.S. journalist and television host Savannah Guthrie, Feb. 5, 2026. (Reuters/Rebecca Noble)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

At least one suspect was recorded by Guthrie's Nest doorbell camera. According to the FBI, he is between 5 feet, 9 inches and 5 feet, 10 inches tall with a medium build. He was wearing a mask, long sleeves and gloves, and the backpack he carried has been identified as a black Ozark Trail bag.
The family is urging anyone with information to dial 1-800-CALL-FBI.
An anonymous reward can be claimed by calling 520-88-CRIME with information that leads to an arrest.

title: Influencer accused of targeting wealthy dating app matches back behind bars
summary: Adva Lavie, also known as Mia Ventura, allegedly cut her ankle monitor while awaiting trial on dating app burglary charges targeting wealthy victims.
story: Elaine Angene Escoe, on the run since May 2025, was captured in Jamaica while living under a fake identity of 'Harley Newman' and returned to the United States today to face justice. FBI Director Kash Patel emphasized the historic success of the 'Most Wanted Fraudster' list, noting Escoe is the fourth such capture in five weeks.
A Los Angeles influencer accused of targeting wealthy victims before stealing from them is back behind bars after authorities said she allegedly removed her ankle monitor while awaiting trial.
Adva Lavie, 28, who also goes by Mia Ventura, was arrested Tuesday night in Beverly Hills just months after she was released on electronic monitoring while awaiting trial on felony burglary charges.

Prosecutors said Lavie violated the conditions of her release by allegedly removing the electronic monitor she was ordered to wear. A judge has since revoked her release, ordered her held without bail and scheduled a bail review hearing for Friday in Van Nuys.
Court records also show Lavie was arrested on an outstanding Riverside County warrant in a separate grand theft case.
NEARLY 1 IN 12 DEFENDANTS ON ANKLE MONITORS IN CHICAGO HAVE GONE AWOL, AUTHORITIES SAY
Adva Lavie, also known as Mia Ventura, is shown in a Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department special bulletin. (Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department)

Newly obtained court records show Riverside County prosecutors charged Lavie in April with felony grand theft after accusing her of stealing more than $11,000 in luxury items during the 2025 Coachella Music Festival.

Prosecutors said Lavie failed to appear for her scheduled May arraignment, prompting a judge to issue a $20,000 arrest warrant. As of Thursday afternoon, she had not yet been booked into Riverside County, and no in-custody arraignment had been scheduled.
HOMEOWNERS IN LEAFY ENCLAVES HIT BY BURGLARS ZEROING IN ON HIGH-END HOMES FOR SMASH-AND-GRAB SCORES

Adva Lavie, also known as Mia Ventura, is shown in a Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department special bulletin alongside vehicles authorities said were linked to a residential burglary series targeting victims through dating apps. (Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department)

The Riverside case centers on allegations Lavie stole an approximately $8,600 Rolex watch, Louis Vuitton Aviator sunglasses valued at about $700 and a Louis Vuitton cardholder worth about $1,800 from a man she attended Coachella with.

Investigators said the man invited Lavie to stay with him at an Airbnb in Indio during Coachella weekend. After the pair argued, she allegedly helped herself to the luxury items from his unlocked Tesla Cybertruck before leaving.

According to an arrest warrant, surveillance cameras at the Airbnb captured the alleged theft, and detectives later identified Lavie from the video. Investigators also noted she was a suspect in another theft reported at the same property.
FLORIDA MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY LURED WOMEN WITH DATING APP COULD HAVE MORE VICTIMS: AUTHORITIES
Adva Lavie, also known as Mia Ventura, in modeling photos. (Paul Archuleta/Getty Images for Teatro Live; Paul Archuleta/Getty Images)
Lavie's latest arrest comes nearly four months after Los Angeles County prosecutors accused her of carrying out a dating app burglary spree targeting wealthy victims across Southern California.

Prosecutors allege Lavie spent years using dating apps and "Sugar Daddy" websites to build relationships with wealthy older men and younger women before posing as a girlfriend or travel companion to gain access to their homes.
Adva Lavie, also known as Mia Ventura, in red carpet and event photos. (Paul Archuleta/Getty Images; Paul Archuleta/Getty Images for Teatro Live; Paul Archuleta/Getty Images for Teatro)
Once inside, authorities said, she stole cash, gold, credit cards and luxury designer items from victims in Westlake Village, West Hollywood, Los Angeles and Beverly Hills.

Lavie has pleaded not guilty to six felony charges, including two counts of grand theft, two counts of first-degree residential burglary and two counts of unauthorized use of personal identifying information. She was released from custody on an electronic ankle monitor before her latest arrest.
When announcing the case in March, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said prosecutors intended to prove Lavie exploited the trust she built through online relationships.
Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman speaks at a news conference alongside Los Angeles County Sheriff Robert Luna June 11, 2025, in Los Angeles. (KTTV)

"At her trial, we will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that this defendant exploited trust built through online relationships to gain access to victims' homes and steal from them," Hochman said. "Her ability to deceptively influence others, whether in person or online, has now come to an end."

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department previously released a public bulletin identifying Lavie as the suspect in the dating app burglary investigation and published photographs of luxury vehicles investigators said she drove, including a white Mercedes-Benz coupe and a black Porsche SUV.

Fox 11 Los Angeles previously reported that Lavie's fiancé, billionaire entrepreneur Stephen Cloobeck, was arrested on separate felony charges alleging he attempted to dissuade witnesses from testifying against her.

If convicted on all six felony counts in the Los Angeles County case, Lavie faces up to 11 years and eight months in state prison.
Fox News Digital's Michael Dorgan contributed to this report.
