She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Freed American reveals brutal Iran prison ordeal, warns hostages face greater danger
summary: Morad Tahbaz describes harsh Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps detention in Evin Prison and warns that the U.S.-Iran war could make Americans still held in Tehran more vulnerable.
story: Morad Tahbaz, who spent nearly six years in Evin Prison, says Western governments have failed to deter Iran’s hostage-taking and warns renewed conflict could worsen conditions for Americans still held.

For nearly six years, American conservationist Morad Tahbaz lived in what he described as hell inside Iran’s prison system. The worst four months were spent completely alone in a small cell, beneath a bright light that never went dark.
Tahbaz was held in Ward 2A of Iran’s Evin Prison, which he described as a high-security detention facility controlled by the intelligence branch of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

He was allowed out only twice a day for about 10 minutes and was forced to wear a blindfold whenever he left, Tahbaz told Fox News Digital. His weekly call with his wife lasted only a few minutes and was monitored so closely that an official interrupted whenever he spoke in English.

"This is probably the harshest and toughest imprisonment that any prisoner will go through," Tahbaz, who was finally released in September 2023, told Fox News Digital of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps intelligence detention facility inside Iran's Evin Prison.
WHO IS AHMAD VAHIDI? IRAN’S NEW IRGC CHIEF TIED TO GLOBAL ATTACKS AND ‘DEATH TO AMERICA’ IDEOLOGY

Morad Tahbaz, an Iranian American conservationist, in Golestan National Park, Iran. Tahbaz spent nearly six years in Iran’s Evin Prison before being released with four other Americans in September 2023. (Morad Tahbaz)

Tahbaz was living in the U.S. and working in Iran as a conservationist when authorities arrested him alongside several colleagues in January 2018. He had co-founded the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation, which worked to protect endangered species including the Asiatic cheetah and Persian leopard.
One of the accusations leveled against him, Tahbaz said, was that he had trained lizards to spy on Iranian military installations for Israel.

"You can’t make this stuff up," Tahbaz said in the Zoom interview with Fox News Digital. "It just gives you an idea of the kind of narrative that this regime comes up with. They’ll come up with anything."
What began with interrogations in January 2018 turned into nearly six years of imprisonment for the Iranian American conservationist.

Now free and back in his home in the U.S., Tahbaz fears the war between the United States and Iran could make the Americans still held by Iran both more vulnerable and more valuable as negotiating assets.
"I do think the strikes in Iran will have an impact on the hostages’ situation and their circumstances," he said.
TRUMP SAYS IRAN WILL PAY — WHAT IT TAKES TO END THE WAR REMAINS UNCLEAR
Morad Tahbaz reunites with his family following his release from Iran in September 2023. (Morad Tahbaz)
Tahbaz said he spent his first two years inside the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps intelligence facility at Evin.
After his conviction, Tahbaz was transferred into the general prison population. He said his cellmates ranged from suspected ISIS members to former Iranian government ministers.
The isolation and physical conditions were accompanied by constant uncertainty.

"The uncertainty when you are a hostage is not like you think at the end of your sentence they’ll necessarily let you go," Tahbaz said. "They’ll just come up with another charge to keep you there for as long as you’re of value to them."

Tahbaz was released Sept. 18, 2023, with four other Americans in a Qatar-mediated agreement between Washington and Iran. The exchange also involved five Iranians held by the United States and the transfer of $6 billion in previously frozen Iranian funds into a restricted account for humanitarian transactions.
The negotiation brought Tahbaz home, but he believes Western governments have failed to establish consequences strong enough to stop Iran from detaining more foreign and dual nationals.
"This business of hostage-taking has been going on essentially since the beginning of the revolution," he said.
LAWYER FOR AMERICAN DETAINED IN IRAN SAYS HOSTAGE DEAL IS 'EASIEST PROBLEM ON THE TABLE' FOR BOTH SIDES
Freed hostage Morad Tahbaz is surrounded by his family just after landing in the U.S. in September 2023. (Morad Tahbaz)
"It will continue, in my opinion, as long as there is no deterrence," Tahbaz added. "None of the Western governments, in reality, have done anything significant about stopping this practice."
The issue returned to the forefront in July with the release of Dena Karari, a 53-year-old Iranian American from California.

Karari had been unable to leave Iran since December 2024 after authorities confiscated her passports. Her attorney said she faced allegations of espionage and collaboration with a hostile state. President Donald Trump announced in July that she had been allowed to leave and called the decision a "gesture of goodwill."
Karari was not continuously imprisoned, according to reporting about her case, but she remained under an exit ban and was repeatedly interrogated.
Her release offered relief during a widening conflict, but Tahbaz said dual nationals remain particularly vulnerable because Iran does not recognize their foreign citizenship.
"Iran doesn’t recognize any other nationality other than the Iranian," he said.
Authorities can develop a national-security case, secure a sentence and then preserve the prisoner for use in future negotiations, Tahbaz said.
"You’re condemned, and they pass sentence, and you’re in the system, and now you are a bargaining chip," he said.
The precise number of Americans currently imprisoned or prevented from leaving Iran remains unclear.

Reuters reported in March that at least six U.S. citizens or permanent residents were detained in Iran, including journalist Reza Valizadeh, businessman Kamran Hekmati and U.S. permanent resident Shahab Dalili.
A view of the entrance of Evin prison in Tehran, Iran Oct. 17, 2022. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via Reuters)

Valizadeh, a former Radio Farda journalist, was sentenced to 10 years for allegedly collaborating with a hostile government. Hekmati was sentenced to two years for having visited Israel more than a decade earlier, according to his family. Dalili, who was arrested after traveling to Iran for his father’s funeral, was sentenced to 10 years for allegedly cooperating with a hostile government.
Advocates warned that escalating strikes could increase the risk that detainees would be harmed or used as leverage.
The State Department formally designated Hekmati, who has bladder cancer, as wrongfully detained in March.

Tahbaz said he believes three Americans remain in custody, although that number could not be independently confirmed. Some cases are deliberately kept private because families fear publicity could increase the danger to detainees.
His concerns about the current war are rooted in how Iranian interrogators responded to tensions with Washington during his own imprisonment.

"When I was taken in in January of 2018, and it was right at the beginning of the first Trump administration, the amount of frustration and anger at the rollback of the JCPOA at that time, I mean, it was thrown into my face just about every day of my interrogation in some way, shape or form," Tahbaz said, referring to a 2015 nuclear deal, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action.
The United States formally withdrew from the 2015 nuclear agreement, known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, in May 2018, several months after Tahbaz’s arrest.
Tahbaz believes the current conflict could similarly be transferred onto prisoners who have no control over decisions made in Washington.
"It definitely will worsen the case of prisoners in custody and those who may be just under surveillance or potential hostages," he said.
US ‘LOCKED AND LOADED’ FOR ‘MUCH HIGHER’ STRIKES IF IRAN TALKS FAIL AS TRUMP PAUSES HORMUZ OPS

Morad Tahbaz with Eskandar Firouz, the founding head of Iran’s Department of the Environment, at Lar National Park in Iran. Firouz, who was imprisoned for six years following the 1979 revolution, died several years after the photo was taken. (Morad Tahbaz)
He described prisoners as one more source of leverage in Iran’s broader confrontation with the United States.
"You’re seeing that playing out even with the war, this tit-for-tat, you do this, we’ll do that," he said.
"The hostages are, you know, just a commodity from Iran’s perspective, to be used at the right time."
Tahbaz’s experience with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps also shapes his analysis of the struggle unfolding inside Iran.
He stressed that he is not a political analyst and described his conclusions as personal assessments based on his experience and conversations with contacts familiar with the country.
Tahbaz said he believes competing interests within the Revolutionary Guard are fighting to preserve their political and economic power.

He pointed specifically to Khatam al-Anbiya, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' engineering and construction conglomerate. Tahbaz argued that sanctions have benefited powerful IRGC-linked entities by forcing oil sales, imports and money transfers into opaque black and gray markets.
"They have created a huge franchise for themselves because of these sanctions," he said.
"They don’t want to see the sanctions go away, because they will lose their franchise, if you will. They will lose their power, their control over the money and everything that goes along with it."
He said ordinary Iranians have suffered most from the resulting economic isolation and wartime conditions.
"The people who are hurt most by all of this are the people of Iran," Tahbaz said. "They’re unfortunately taking the brunt of all of these in their daily lives."
Tahbaz predicted Iranians would eventually return to the streets, but said many had lost confidence that Western governments would intervene to help remove the regime.
"I’m sure they’ll be back on the streets," he said. "But I think this notion that the Western states are going to step in and help them overthrow this regime, that went out the window."

Tahbaz said many Iranians had previously been strongly sympathetic toward the United States and initially hoped the conflict might end the Islamic Republic. That characterization reflects his assessment and conversations and could not be independently quantified.
He believes any future political movement will have to develop primarily inside Iran rather than being directed by opposition groups abroad.
"There’s a lot of hatred and anger just boiling there," Tahbaz said. "So it will boil up and over again without a doubt. The question is when, how, but it will happen again."

Tahbaz is recounting his imprisonment in his new book, "Green Parrots: A Memoir of Survival in Iran’s Evin Prison," scheduled for publication Sept. 18. The publisher says the book describes how he relied on skills developed while tracking endangered wildlife to survive nearly six years in Evin, including solitary confinement.

His release illustrates the contradiction confronting governments trying to recover their citizens: negotiations can bring individual prisoners home, but Tahbaz believes the broader practice will continue unless Iran faces meaningful deterrence for taking them.

Military members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in western Tehran, Iran. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
He survived because governments ultimately negotiated for his freedom.
His warning is that as the war intensifies, the Americans still held in Iran could become more valuable to Tehran at precisely the moment their circumstances become more dangerous.

title: Gunman fired at US consulate in Toronto, second time building was shot at this year
summary: The second shooting at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto this year triggered an hourlong police chase, although no arrest was made as officials continue to investigate.
story: Harris Faulkner speaks with Rep. Rick Crawford R-Ark., chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, about the shooting at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto, Canada.
A gunman fired at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto on Monday, marking the second time this year someone shot at the building, according to authorities.
A single shell casing was found at the scene, and there was damage to the building's facade.
No injuries were reported in the incident.
"The U.S. Embassy and Consulates in Canada are open and operating normally, though some routine U.S. citizen services in Toronto are being rescheduled," the consulate said in a statement.
GUNFIRE SHATTERS TORONTO LATIN STREET FESTIVAL, LEAVING AT LEAST 2 DEAD AND MULTIPLE WOUNDED
Police at the scene of a shooting outside the U.S. Consulate in Toronto, on Monday, July 27, 2026. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press via AP)

Toronto Deputy Police Chief Frank Barredo said there was a high-speed chase after the shooting that lasted an hour. However, no arrest was made and Barredo committed to continuing the search for those involved.
"We will approach this investigation with great seriousness," Barredo said at a news conference. "We will bring the people responsible for this to justice."
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow described the shooting as a "brazen attack."
"I want to say to the person or persons responsible, we will get you," she said.

This was the second shooting targeting the U.S. Consulate this year, with the first coming on March 10, when two suspects allegedly fired multiple shots at the building before driving away in a stolen vehicle.
Toronto Police Deputy Chief Frank Barredo at a press conference after a shot was fired at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto, on Monday, July 27, 2026. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press via AP)
Sheldon Tracy-Stewart, 18, and Zara Jabbi, 19, were arrested last month and charged with multiple offenses in connection with the March shooting. The allegations have not been tested in court.
A police presence has been seen at the consulate since the first shooting.
Barredo said a patrol vehicle was outside the consulate with its lights on when the shooting happened. Two security personnel were also in the building.
Last month, police said they believed multiple shootings, including the one in March, could be tied to "multilayered" gun-for-hire networks that have also targeted Toronto synagogues.
Two popular Jewish-owned bakeries were targeted by gunfire over the weekend.
US CONSULATE IN TORONTO STRUCK BY GUNFIRE, POLICE SAY; NO INJURIES REPORTED
Police are investigating after a shot was fired at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto, on Monday, July 27, 2026. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press via AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Barredo said police had not ruled out a connection between Monday's consulate shooting and the attacks on the bakeries. The motive for the consulate shooting remains under investigation.
"Investigators will follow the evidence to where it leads," he said.
Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario, said he was "disgusted" by the recent violence in Toronto.

"I’m totally disgusted by the shootings and vandalism that took place in Toronto over the last few days, including at two Jewish-owned businesses over the weekend and near the U.S. Consulate this morning," he said on X. "In all cases, active police investigations are underway. I expect all those responsible to be found, prosecuted and punished to the fullest extent of the law."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Christian persecution concerns rise in Egypt as State Department presses religious freedom
summary: Egypt's 20 million Coptic Christians face discrimination and occasional violence as experts say the state fails to address anti-Christian fanaticism seriously.
story: The Middle East experiences a significant spiritual shift as millions of Muslims convert to Christianity, a phenomenon tracked by Open Doors. Pastor Georges Houssney of Horizons International shares his 50 years of experience ministering in the region, detailing how many are disillusioned with Islam due to war and receiving visions of Christ, even risking death in Iran.

A series of violent attacks on Egyptian Christians, including the incarceration of a man who converted from Islam to Christianity, prompted the U.S. State Department to urge that religious freedom be respected in the Muslim-majority country of Egypt.
The situation of the Christian minority in Egypt has implications for religious freedom in the northern African nation that receives $1.3 billion in annual funding from the U.S.

Raymond Ibrahim, an expert on Christians in the Muslim world, wrote on the website of the Gatestone Institute, that "Said Mansour Rezk Abdelrazek, a Muslim convert to Christianity, has become one of Egypt's most prominent religious freedom cases.
NIGERIAN PASTOR HIGHLIGHTED BY TRUMP SAYS HE’S NEXT AFTER MILITIA KILLS HIS RELATIVES

"After embracing Christianity in 2016, he endured years of harassment, detention, and abuse. On April 13, prosecutors referred him to a terrorism court, while his lawyers were denied access to the case file. He remains imprisoned, with advocates reporting torture, physical abuse, denial of adequate medical care, and repeated postponements of his trial."

In another case, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR) reported that a mob of Muslims tossed stones at a church in Upper Egypt on July 8, injuring Christians and causing damage to the building and a priest’s car.
Just days later, a group of men attacked the Rev. Matta Roushdy, 49, a priest at the Virgin Mary and St. Abanoub Coptic Orthodox Church in Dahab, South Sinai Governorate.
REPORT DETAILS RISING PRESSURE ON UNDERGROUND CATHOLICS AS CHINA DENIES CRACKDOWN

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital that President Donald Trump has stated, "America will always defend the right of every person to live out their faith openly, freely, and without fear." The spokesperson added, "Religious freedom is a fundamental American value. We aspire for all others to enjoy the same freedom, protection, and benefits."

However, there has been some progress in combating bias against Coptic Christians. The organization Coptic Solidarity wrote last week that a breakthrough unfolded with respect to the alleged longstanding discrimination against Coptic athletes in soccer.
Egyptian Coptic Christians attend the Resurrection Mass at the Monastery of St. Simon Al-Kharaz during Holy Saturday services on April 19, 2025, in Cairo, Egypt. (Ahmad Hasaballah/Getty Images)

"In an unprecedented move, Egypt’s Ministry of Youth and Sports announced that its investigation found sufficient evidence of misconduct by a coach at Alexandria’s Al-Ittihad Club who allegedly excluded a junior football player, Makari Younan, because of his Christian name," the organization announced.

It added, "The decision deserves recognition. Whether motivated by public pressure or a genuine policy shift, the Ministry’s response represents a notable departure from the longstanding official tendency to dismiss such allegations."
CHRISTIAN SCHOOL CHAPLAIN WINS SETTLEMENT AFTER FIRING OVER LGBTQ SERMON

The organization continued, "It appears to be the first official acknowledgment that discrimination against Copts in Egyptian sport is not merely an allegation raised by disappointed families or human rights organizations, but a matter requiring government intervention."

Open Doors, a global organization that aids persecuted Christians around the world, said of the attack on the priest, "These types of attacks are usually committed by members of radical Islamist groups such as the Muslim Brotherhood."

Their statement added, "Their actions reflect a broader anti-Christian sentiment, especially in rural and village societies across the country where weak law enforcement leaves Christians vulnerable to attack. Though violent cases like this have decreased in the last decade, these attacks will continue until the state takes anti-Christian fanaticism as seriously as it deserves."
Fox News Digital sent multiple press query emails to the Egyptian embassies in Washington and Tel Aviv and called the embassy in Washington.

Coptic Orthodox Christians gather for an Easter service at the Monastery of St. Simon the Tanner, located in the Mokattam Mountain area of Cairo on April 19, 2025. (Ahmed Sayed/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Dalia Ziada, an Egyptian Middle East scholar and research fellow at the Institute for the Study of Global Antisemitism and Policy, told Fox News Digital, "These cases represent only a small fraction of what Coptic Christians endure in Egypt every day. We are speaking about a population of more than 20 million Egyptians. On paper, they are labeled a minority. In reality, they are at the essence of Egyptian identity. They are the preservers of the country’s history and cultural memory."

According to Ziada, "Women and Coptic Christians constitute President El-Sisi’s most important political base. These were the two vulnerable groups that felt most threatened by the Muslim Brotherhood in the aftermath of the Arab Spring. They strongly supported El-Sisi then, and they continue to support him today. Consequently, he must maintain the appearance of protecting and pleasing them by visiting their church on Christmas every year. But beyond that, nothing is actually happening to make them less vulnerable."
The U.S. State Department 2025 report on Christians depicts a bleak situation for the Egyptian Christian community. The community makes up an estimated 10% of the nation’s 120 million people.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

According to the State Department report on Egyptian Christians, "Despite efforts for greater representation, Christians remain underrepresented in senior positions across the public sector. Currently, only two Christians – the minister of local development and the minister of parliamentary affairs – serve in Egypt’s 31-member cabinet," wrote the State Department, adding: "Of 27 appointed governors, only one is Christian. In the senate, 24 Christians (17 elected and seven appointed) hold seats, out of 300 senators. One serves as deputy speaker. A Coptic Christian is the head of the constitutional court. No Christian serves as president of any of the country’s 27 public universities. Employment discrimination against Christians – especially within the security services, judiciary, and senior civil service – remains a significant issue."

According to an April 29 Christian Today report, a Coptic Christian YouTuber, Augustinos Samaan, was sentenced to five years in prison for insulting Islam because he published videos defending the Christian faith.

title: Hackers targeted municipal water systems in 7 states this week, FBI says
summary: Cyberattacks targeting municipal water systems have been reported in at least seven states this week, prompting the FBI and the Environmental Protection Agency to warn utilities nationwide that hackers are trying to disrupt critical water infrastructure.
story: Cyberattacks targeting municipal water systems have been reported in at least seven states this week, prompting the FBI and the Environmental Protection Agency to warn utilities nationwide that hackers are trying to disrupt critical water infrastructure.

In a public service announcement Thursday, the agencies said water and wastewater utilities have reported incidents to the FBI, with some malicious activity degrading water operations. The announcement does not name the states.

The warning comes after hackers targeted more than 30 municipal water facilities in Minnesota in an attack that had hallmarks of Iranian meddling, according to a law enforcement official. It is still under investigation.

A spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology services agency said Thursday there was no indication the breaches contaminated any municipal water supplies. The federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said in a separate alert that some larger attacks on water infrastructure had “resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations,” though it did not say where.

Minnesota officials and the U.S. government have not publicly attributed the malicious activity in the state to a specific actor. Likewise, the FBI and the EPA did not identify a culprit behind the breaches in the other states.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters Friday at Camp David, blamed Minnesota’s leaders and Gov. Tim Walz, who was the Democratic vice presidential nominee in the 2024 election.

“I think I blame it on Minnesota because they’re grossly incompetent,” Trump said. “I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota. They like to say, ‘Oh, it’s Iran.’ Iran should be so lucky. Iran’s got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota.”

In response to a request for comment, Walz said in part: “Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too. This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there’s no plan to win a war with Iran.”
The FBI and EPA advisory focused less on attribution than on the tactics used in the attacks.

The federal advisory said the malicious cyber actors, or MCAs, targeted specific brands of control systems used by municipal water utilities, though the FBI and the EPA urged operators of all systems to take precautions.

Earlier this week, the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources issued a bulletin to water contacts in the state, saying  intelligence officials believed that “systems within Wisconsin may be susceptible to connections from malicious cyber actors.”
“This leads us to believe that the cyber threat is ongoing in Wisconsin and requires immediate action to prevent potentially serious impacts to our systems,” the bulletin said.

A Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources spokesperson emphasized that intelligence officials in the state “had not yet confirmed that systems in Wisconsin have had connections but are concerned that they might be susceptible to connections from malicious cyber actors.”
In the warning, Wisconsin said that Minnesota had reported that hackers managed to drop system pressures, which in “several incidents triggered alarms and prompted a response from law enforcement.”
In an email, the spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology agency disputed Wisconsin’s characterizations of the attack and its observed impacts.
“Minnesota has not reported that threat actors lowered pressure across multiple water systems or that pressure changes prompted a law enforcement response,” said the spokesperson, Emily Zimmer.
The agencies said the hackers remotely accessed internet-facing devices, changed IP addresses and passwords, and caused utilities to lose monitoring and control capabilities.

The federal advisory calls on system operators to remove programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, from direct internet exposure by putting them behind secure gateways and firewalls; use strong passwords; and limit communications between authorized control system devices through access control lists.

“Attribution requires careful analysis of technical evidence alongside broader national and international threat intelligence, and our federal partners are best positioned to lead that work,” Zimmer, the spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology agency, said.

The breach in Minnesota happened just days after U.S. officials publicly warned that Iran-backed hackers were targeting the nation’s critical infrastructure amid the escalating military conflict between Washington and Tehran.

In a public advisory July 22, CISA, as well as the FBI and other federal agencies, urged companies to boost their defenses, saying Tehran-linked hackers were trying to breach online automated devices used to manage infrastructure systems.
U.S. intelligence agencies have also cautioned that Iran is increasingly able and willing to carry out aggressive cyber operations and that it tried to target water systems in 2023.

Bryson Bort, the founder of the cybersecurity company Scythe and an expert in industrial control system security, said the FBI’s disclosures this week underscore the need for more public awareness of the risks posed by infrastructure breaches.
“We need to be prepared,” Bort said. “Attacks like this illustrate that there are folks who mean the U.S. harm today.”

title: Trump says he’ll revive ‘anti-weaponization’ fund if Blanche’s nomination for AG is blocked
summary: Trump threatened to “push hard” to keep a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund active, amid an ongoing feud between two Republican senators and the Trump administration over Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general.
story: President Donald Trump on Saturday threatened to “push hard” to keep a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund active, amid an ongoing feud between two Republican senators and the Trump administration over the president’s nomination of Todd Blanche for attorney general.

“If Senators Cornyn and Tillis, both upset because I wouldn’t Endorse them (they lost, and quit, respectively!), aren’t going to approve Todd Blanche, one of the most respected professionals, according to everybody, in the Country, to be the United States Attorney General, then I will keep Todd as Acting A.G., and push hard to get the Anti-Weaponization Bill, which takes care of those who have been so badly treated by the Crooked Joe Biden (and Obuma!) Administration (I get nothing, although I was treated horribly!), PASSED,” the president wrote in a post on Truth Social.
“Todd Blanche was a voice of reason! It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done. Thank you for your attention to this matter!” he added.

Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., are both departing Congress after feuding with Trump. In Texas, Cornyn ran for re-election, losing in a primary runoff to state Attorney General Ken Paxton after Trump endorsed Paxton.
Tillis, in North Carolina, opted not to run for re-election, making his plans to retire public one day after drawing Trump’s ire for opposing a GOP-backed domestic policy package.

The two senators have partially conditioned their support for Blanche’s nomination on the Trump administration rescinding its plans for the fund, which would provide compensation for Jan. 6 rioters pardoned by Trump for claims of government overreach.
In a post on X following Trump’s statement Saturday, Tillis blamed the president for Blanche’s stalled confirmation.

“Despite comments as late as yesterday that the fund is dead, President Trump clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against,” he wrote.
“It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal. Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday,” Tillis added.

Blanche’s nomination has been in jeopardy for several weeks, with Cornyn and Tillis previously saying that there are other Republican senators that share their concerns but don’t sit on the Judiciary Committee and wouldn’t have the chance to vote for or against Blanche until his nomination came to the floor.
On Wednesday night, the committee postponed a vote on Blanche’s nomination because of Cornyn and Tillis’ concerns.
On Friday, at a Cabinet meeting, the president defended the fund, saying, “It is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t.”
“This has nothing to do with Todd,” Trump added.
The anti-weaponization fund has been blocked indefinitely by a federal judge, but the Trump administration has not pledged to stop pursuing it.

The fund was part of a settlement agreement that stemmed from a lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS. Also part of that settlement was an agreement that made the president and several family members immune from IRS audits, another provision that Cornyn and Tillis have shared concerns about.
Earlier this week, the president threatened to withdraw Blanche’s nomination and resubmit it next year, after Tillis and Cornyn have left office.

“Hey, in 158 days they can try it again, roll the dice on what the Senate confirmation process looks like next year,” Tillis told reporters at the Capitol after that threat. “It’s all on him. Certainly within his authority to do that.”

title: Nicole ‘Snooki’ Polizzi reveals hysterectomy after cervical cancer diagnosis
summary: An emotional Nicole “Snooki” Polizzi announced on Friday that she underwent a hysterectomy operation to treat Stage 1 cervical cancer, months after first disclosing her diagnosis.
story: An emotional Nicole “Snooki” Polizzi announced on Friday that she underwent a hysterectomy operation to treat Stage 1 cervical cancer, months after first disclosing her diagnosis.

The reality star, who earned fame as a hard-partying roommate on MTV’s “Jersey Shore,” announced her health scare earlier this year. Polizzi, 38, credited regular Pap smears with catching her cancer early and encouraged other women to keep up with their own exams for early detection.

Gynecologists use Pap smears to identify irregular cervical cells that can signal cancer or develop into the disease. A hysterectomy is the surgical removal of the uterus and can treat conditions ranging from cancer to endometriosis and fibroids.

“I’m going to be honest with you — not great,” Polizzi said in a TikTok post from her recovery bed. “I told you guys, in general I’m not good with pain and I’ve really been trying to be tough, but it’s not great.”

Polizzi documented her surgery experience on TikTok, from her drive to the hospital with her parents to the moment her stretcher was wheeled into the operating room. According to Polizzi, doctors also repaired her abdominal wall and performed a partial vaginal removal during the procedure.

The TV personality and businesswoman has used her platform to raise awareness about the disease and the importance of routine screening. Polizzi broke down in her video message to followers but said she was trying to stay strong.
“The nurses, they’re great. They’re saying I’m going to do fine,” she said through tears, recalling the moments before her operation. “So I lay down and I’m like, f---, it’s happening.”
“Love you! Strongest badass — it’s over and now on the road to recovery,” Polizzi’s “Jersey Shore” co-star Sammi “Sweetheart” Giancola wrote in a comment.
Pap smears are a routine, minimally invasive component of women’s health exams. When they reveal abnormal cells, physicians can monitor the situation for potential problems.
Cervical cancer rates remain a concern for researchers and advocates. The American Cancer Society found cervical cancer diagnosis rose 2% annually among women in their 30s and 40s from 2012 to 2019.

Polizzi has not publicly discussed the cause of her cancer. HPV is considered the primary cause of cervical cancers. About eight in 10 women will have an HPV infection before age 50, according to the Mount Sinai Tisch Cancer Center. Many cases of HPV resolve on their own.

title: FIFA president nixes idea to sell stakes in World Cup to private equity investors
summary: FIFA President Gianni Infantino said Friday he’s nixing a much-criticized plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private equity investors.
story: The president of World Cup organizer FIFA said Friday he’s nixing a much-criticized plan to sell stakes in soccer’s biggest tournament to private equity investors.
The plan to consolidate FIFA’s commercial and event operations into a new commercial subsidiary valued at $20 billion is off the table, FIFA President Gianni Infantino said in a statement.
Asia’s soccer body joined European and North American organizations in opposing it this week, with Europe’s soccer body saying it “will not participate in FIFA competitions” as a result of the plan.
FIFA initially responded by saying in a statement that “nobody is selling football.”
Later on Friday, Infantino said the plan was to strengthen such bodies, not divide world soccer.

“Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place,” he said. “Our purpose has always been — and will always be — to unite and improve.”
The plan, called FIFA Forward Enterprise, inspired Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker and officially Infantino’s senior adviser, to resign.
“I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup,” he said in a statement.

Such a move would have provided a one-time payment of $20 million to each FIFA member federation. North America’s CONCACAF (Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football) rejected it.

Infantino on Friday said his “intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.”

title: Trump appeals ruling that found his $10B IRS suit aimed to ‘manipulate’ legal proceedings
summary: The case is at the center of negotiations between two Republican senators and the Justice Department over Todd Blanche’s nomination to serve as attorney general.
story: President Donald Trump on Friday took the first step in appealing a federal judge’s ruling that questioned the legality of a lawsuit filed by the president, two of his sons and the Trump Organization against the IRS.

The Trumps filed notice that they would appeal the July 13 ruling by U.S. District Judge Kathleen Williams that said the $10 billion suit was for an “improper purpose.” The case led to the Justice Department creating a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund as part of a settlement that included an agreement that the government would not investigate or seek any sort of payment from the president, his family members and companies on pending tax claims.
The IRS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the forthcoming appeal.

A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said Friday that the IRS “wrongly allowed a rogue, politically-motivated employee to leak private and confidential information about President Trump, his family, and the Trump Organization” to news outlets that was later “illegally released to millions of people.”
A former IRS contractor pleaded guilty in 2023 to stealing Trump’s tax records and thousands of others in 2019 and 2020 before leaking them. He is serving a five-year prison term.

The president sued the IRS and the Treasury Department in January over allegations that the agency was at fault for an unauthorized release of his tax documents that led to a report in The New York Times that said Trump had paid only $750 in federal income taxes in 2016 and 2017.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google

In her ruling, Williams, a Barack Obama appointee, said Trump sued the IRS over his leaked tax records to “manipulate the judicial process” rather than to “vindicate rights.” She also pointed out that Trump has jurisdiction over the Justice Department, Treasury Department and the IRS.

The ruling said the Justice Department could not portray the settlement with Trump as a judicial agreement. The judge also ordered sanctions against acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, a former personal lawyer to Trump, and Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, in addition to asking the Florida Bar Association to consider whether disciplinary action was necessary for one of Trump’s attorneys, Alejandro Brito.
The unprecedented settlement is at the center of a standoff between two Republican senators and the Justice Department that has stalled a vote on Blanche’s nomination for attorney general.

Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., have demanded that the DOJ agree to permanently shut down the “anti-weaponization” fund and narrow the audit protection deal before they will commit to advancing Blanche’s nomination.

Trump on Friday morning acknowledged the fund is dead but told reporters, “I wish it weren’t.” He did not answer a question about whether he’d agree to limit the terms of the tax deal for himself, his family and his company.

title: The internet is obsessed with Jellycats, but are they worth the splurge? We tested them to find out
summary: Jellycat plushies are all over TikTok, but are they worth $25 to $100 a pop? NBC Selected editors share their honest, firsthand take on the popular toy brand.
story: If you’ve spent any time on TikTok or wandered past a display of impossibly soft stuffed animals at a gift shop, you’ve probably met a Jellycat. The British brand has become one of the most collected (and gifted) soft toy lines around, with fans anticipating new “drops” the same way sneakerheads camp out for limited releases.

With the classic Bashful Bunny, the ever-expanding Amuseables food and object collection, and characters like a plush turtle that’s considerably grumpy, Jellycat has built a cult following among babies, teens and adults alike. Even scoring a reservation at the brand’s Jellycat Diner inside New York City’s iconic toy store FAO Schwartz rivals some of the best restaurants in Manhattan (rather than actual food, you’ll see adorable culinary-themed plushies on the menu).

But with prices that can range from $25 for a small Amuseable to $70 for the diner experience and over $100 for bigger stuffies, is a Jellycat actually worth it, or are you just paying for the name? To find out, I turned to other NBC Selected editors who are well versed in the Jellycat world.

Jellycat’s Bashful Bunny is the toy that built the brand’s reputation, and it’s easy to see why. The fur is dense but not stiff and the actual bunny is stuffed enough that it feels plush to hug (but not so much that it feels too firm to cuddle with). It comes in more than a dozen colors, including the original beige, blush, lilac and cream, plus seasonal variations that show up and sell out fast.

My mom bought my daughter a now-sold-out version of this bunny with floral fabric sewn into its ears when she was first born. Five years later, the bunny is still one of her favorite stuffies. I’ve washed it a number of times and it still looks great; it looks well-loved, but still holding its shape. The floppy limbs and beanbag-weighted bottom also make it comfortable to hold or prop up.

They make especially good gifts for loved ones. “While Jellycats are pretty pricey, I find the keychains to be a good entry point,” says NBC Selected contributor Marilyn La Jeunesse. “I like that they can come along with you on all your adventures. Plus, I love knowing that if I travel to London, Paris, Seoul, or Shanghai, I can stop by and pick up an exclusive style sold only in that city. It’s like a worldwide treasure hunt.” For those not in the know, there are exclusive Jellycats available in different countries and at different retailers. You can use it to stash small essentials like your lip balm and hand lotion, or to organize your chargers while traveling. The pouch is relatively small and just big enough to fit an iPhone, wallet and a few other small items.

Candidly, I tend to lean practical over cutesy when it comes to my accessories, but I grabbed this pouch for myself when shopping for stuffies with my daughter and love it. It stands out in my tote, so I never have to dig deep to grab it,  and it adds a moment of joy to my day anytime I pull it out. It’s also a great conversation starter; I’ve had so many strangers stop and compliment it.
What can improve
While we’ve loved collecting and testing our own Jellycats, there are few things to be aware of:

Inventory is unpredictable. Popular colors and characters sell out quickly and are sometimes retired for good, which drives up resale prices on secondhand marketplaces and can be frustrating if you’re chasing a specific item. Not all lines are equally durable. While Bashful and Fuddlewuddle held up well to washing, a few of the more delicate Amuseables with suedette or felt details can show early signs of wear with heavy handling, according to some of our editors.
How we tried Jellycats

Several NBC Selected editors are longtime Jellycat devotees, so we drew on our own firsthand experience for this story. Between Godio, La Jeunesse and myself, we have 23+ of our own Jellycats, have gifted them to friends and family for birthdays and baby showers, and in my case, watched my own kids grow attached to a few favorites that now rarely leave their sides. That mix of personal collecting, gift-giving and real-world testing (including plenty of tugging, dropping and machine-washing) informed our picks and feedback.
What is Jellycat?

Jellycat is a British plush toy company founded in 1999 by siblings Thomas and William Gatacre. It is known for its distinctively soft and often whimsical stuffed animals — think plump sushi rolls, wedges of cheese, and bug-eyed amphibians alongside more traditional bunnies and bears. Based in London, the company has built a cult following among both children and adults, driven in part by its Amuseables line, which turns everyday objects and foods into huggable characters, and by limited releases that sell out quickly and circulate for inflated prices on resale sites. Jellycat toys are sold online and in boutiques, museum gift shops and department stores worldwide.
Who is Jellycat for?

Jellycat makes sense for anyone who wants a stuffed animal that feels a step beyond the average teddy bear you may find at the store. This includes new parents looking for a durable, huggable baby gift, kids who want something to actually love hard and adults who’ve been pulled into the collectible side of the plush world thanks to social media. It’s a genuinely strong pick for gifting across ages, from a newborn’s first Fuddlewuddle to a “get well soon” Amuseable for a friend.
While Jellycats can go for over $100 for some of the larger items, there are options under $30 for those on a budget. This includes some of their smaller plushies and bag charms.

I am a commerce editor at NBC Selected and a journalist who regularly covers wellness, beauty, and lifestyle. I have also written about Labubus, Needoh and Play-Doh for adults. I have two kids — a 5-year-old daughter and 1-year-old son — who are both obsessed with Jellycats. For this story, I relied on my personal experience with the brand and spoke with other NBC Selected editors about their experience with it.
