title: Officer who shot Sonya Massey denied medical release from 20-year prison sentence
summary: Sean Grayson, the man who fatally shot Sonya Massey in her home in 2024, has been denied medical release by the Illinois Prisoner Review Board, a board spokesperson said Friday.
story: Sean Grayson, the man who fatally shot Sonya Massey in her home in 2024, has been denied medical release by the Illinois Prisoner Review Board, a board spokesperson said Friday.
Grayson, in a medical release request application obtained by NBC News via a Freedom of Information Act request, had asked to end his 20-year prison sentence after serving only six months.
Liz Mitchell, the spokesperson, said in a statement that the board voted 3-0 to deny Grayson’s application, keeping him imprisoned.
But Sangamon County State’s Attorney John C. Milhiser opposed Grayson’s potential release, writing a letter that recalled the facts of the case and stated that Grayson remains a danger to society.

Grayson, a former Sangamon County sheriff’s deputy, was diagnosed with Stage 3 colon cancer in 2023, his attorney, Mark Wykoff said at his sentencing in January, after Grayson was convicted of second-degree murder last year in relation to Massey’s killing.
By the time of the sentencing, the cancer had progressed to Stage 4 and spread to his liver, lungs and rectum. Wykoff worried that prison time would worsen Grayson’s condition.

Grayson filed for release under the Joe Coleman Act, which applies to incarcerated people who are terminally ill or medically incapacitated. The application defines that standard as either having a condition that will not improve or one that prevents someone from performing normal daily living tasks unassisted.

As a part of the application, a medical professional evaluated Grayson and deemed his condition “irreversible and incurable,” checking a box indicating Grayson is likely to die within 18 months due to his cancer.
The doctor did not, however, deem Grayson medically incapacitated, finding that the cancer does not interfere with his ability to take care of himself in daily life.
Grayson killed Massey after she called to report a prowler outside of her home in 2024. He was dispatched to the scene and entered her apartment.

While inside, Massey picked up a pot of boiling water from her stove, prompting Grayson to back away. She asked where he was going, and he replied: “Getting away from your hot steaming water,” according to Milhiser’s recounting.
Massey responded, “Away from my hot steaming water? I rebuke you in the name of Jesus.” When Grayson looked confused, she repeated, “I rebuke you in the name of Jesus.”

Grayson then pointed his gun at Massey and threatened to shoot her. She apologized and dropped to the floor, but he fired the weapon three times, hitting her. As she lay bleeding and struggling to breathe, he declined to offer medical care, Milhiser said. She was later pronounced dead at the hospital.
In a handwritten statement included in the application, Grayson appeared to show little remorse for his actions and maintained that Massey attacked him with the pot of hot water.
“The female Sony (sic) Massey invited me inside,” Grayson wrote, adding, “while inside she attacked me with a pot of boiling water and I fatally shot Ms. Massey.”

Grayson “was already diagnosed with cancer when he shot and killed Sonya Massey in her kitchen. His temper and willingness to escalate minor misunderstandings into fatal encounters shows that he poses a danger to any person he comes into contact with,” Milhiser wrote. “Cancer does not make him less dangerous.”

Milhiser added that Massey’s family also strongly opposed Grayson’s release. During the hearing Sonya Massey’s mother Donna testified telling the judge, “He did it, and I’m done. He did it, and he is a menace to society. He should not be walking around.”

title: F-35 fighter jet crashes in San Diego, sparking fire at Miramar air base
summary: A fighter jet crashed in San Diego on Friday after suffering a “class A mishap,” according to officials.
story: SAN DIEGO — A fighter jet crashed in San Diego on Friday after suffering a “class A mishap,” according to officials.
The F-35B assigned to the 3rd Marine Aircraft Wing of Marine Aircraft Group 11 crashed at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar around 10 a.m. PT, a spokesperson for MCAS Miramar said.

The crash sparked a fire in a field on the base, according to the spokesperson. The base fire department referred inquiries to the MCAS public affairs office, which had no updates on the size of the blaze or when it was knocked down.

The pilot was ejected and taken to a medical facility for evaluation and treatment of injuries believed to be non-life-threatening, the 3rd Marine Aircraft Wing said in a statement. The Marine aviator was said to be stable.
Images of the crash show what appears to be the charred F-35B shrouded in smoke and surrounded by burned grass.
It is unclear what caused the crash.
A spokesperson for the Marine Corps described the crash in a statement as “class A mishap,” the most severe category of military and federal incidents.
The F-35B is a single-seat, short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft with stealth capabilities that can accelerate to 1,200 mph and use temporary airfields and some military vessels.
“It acts as the quarterback of the skies — integrating air, land, sea, space, and cyber operations,” its maker, Lockheed Martin, says in promotional material.
It has helped to replace the British-developed Harrier, phased out in June.
The cost of an F-35B, including spare parts and maintenance, is $135.8 million, according to the nonpartisan Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation.
Marine Aircraft Group 11 provides offense, anti-aircraft warfare, and aerial reconnaissance to U.S. military missions while also training Marine and Navy fighter pilots, according to the corps.
Dennis Romero from San Diego, Matt Lavietes from New York, Mosheh Gains from Washington, D.C.

title: Judge denies request by Elon Musk’s xAI to pause Minnesota nudification ban
summary: A judge denied a request from Elon Musk’s AI company xAI to block Minnesota’s law that will be the first in the nation to ban nudification technology.
story: A federal judge on Friday denied a request from Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI to block a Minnesota law that will be the first in the nation to ban nudification technology.

U.S. District Judge Donovan Frank ruled that there was little risk of immediate harm from the law going into effect as scheduled on Saturday, despite a lawsuit this week from xAI claiming that the law violates the First Amendment’s guarantee of free speech.

“xAI filed the motion on July 29, 2026, nearly three months after the law was signed, and only three days before the law is set to take effect. Such a delay in bringing the action and the motion suggests that harm is not immediate,” the judge wrote in a two-page order, denying xAI’s request for a pause to the law.
The court could still pause the law at a later time. The judge wrote that he’ll hold a hearing on Aug. 19 on whether to grant a preliminary injunction.

The law, which was signed by Democratic Gov. Tim Walz in May, prohibits a person who owns or controls a website, application or software to allow their users to “nudify” images of others. It also prohibits anyone from advertising nudification capabilities.

In its lawsuit filed Monday, Musk’s company did not dispute Minnesota’s interest in banning nudification websites and apps, but said: “The law is overinclusive and there are far less restrictive alternatives that function to achieve the same ends.”

Grok, one of xAI’s products, has faced severe scrutiny for its “Imagine” feature, which uses AI to generate and edit images and videos of users. After the release of a December model, Grok began producing sexualized deepfakes of people with less clothing at the request of users on a massive scale, prompting worldwide outcry and investigations in several jurisdictions. In January, Apple threatened to remove Grok from its app store unless it made changes.
As recently as April, Grok was continuing to generate sexualized images of people without their consent, as users tried to break through restrictions that xAI put in place in January.

Minnesota’s law defines a “nudified” image or video as something that has been “altered or generated to depict an intimate part not depicted in an original unaltered image or video of an identifiable individual.”
The law applies only when “the altered or generated image or video is so realistic that a reasonable person would believe that the intimate part belongs to the identifiable individual.”
In response to the lawsuit, Walz posted on X Tuesday, “See you in court, creep.”

Violating Minnesota’s law could result in a civil penalty of up to $500,000 “for each unlawful access, download or use,” in addition to civil penalties for mental anguish, punitive damages, attorney’s fees or “other relief the court deems just and equitable.” The law says the state’s attorney general may enforce it and that victims may sue on their own. The law does not include criminal penalties.

Keith Ellison, the attorney general of Minnesota, filed a response to xAI’s lawsuit on Friday, urging the court to deny xAI’s request for a temporary restraining order, to convert it into a preliminary injunction motion, and proceed from there. Ellison argued that xAI waited too long — three months after the law was passed — to file an emergency delay, and that its “voluntary delay should not create a manufactured emergency for the Attorney General or the Court.”

xAI’s criticism of the law is drawing support from some free-speech advocates including the American Civil Liberties Union of Minnesota, which supported passage of the law in an earlier form in February but has since turned against it.

“While we believe that creating the technology to alter or ‘nudify’ photos of identifiable people is protected by the First Amendment, we also recognize that the non-consensual creation and dissemination of such material can inflict damage on people appearing in those images,” the ACLU of Minnesota said in a statement Friday.

“In engaging with lawmakers on this issue, we hoped to strike an appropriate balance between First Amendment rights and the ability of people harmed to seek remedial measures, not unlike the remedies available to people harmed by defamation. The final version of the bill does not strike that balance,” the organization said.
xAI argued that it already prohibits users “from generating nude or sexualized images of people without their consent.”

SpaceX, xAI’s parent company, faces class action lawsuits from plaintiffs who claim Grok’s AI chatbot created or shared nude deepfakes of them as children or as adults. The lawsuits also say that xAI failed to alert authorities to the alleged perpetrators who used the tool to create their nude deepfakes.

Minnesota’s law was passed amid wider efforts to regulate AI platforms that can generate deepfakes. In July, San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu sent Apple and Google cease-and-desist letters demanding they remove nudification apps from their app stores.

xAI’s lawsuit argued that creating images and videos using Grok Imagine is a protected First Amendment activity, and that Minnesota’s law did not provide a “safe harbor for good-faith efforts” by companies to avoid nudification efforts.

“Liability attaches even if the depicted persons consented — or created the image themselves — and even if the image is never shared,” xAI’s lawsuit said. “Liability also attaches even if the image has artistic, scientific, political, satirical, educational, medical, or religious value, and (again) even if the company has deployed near-perfect, state-of the-art technical controls to prevent the generation of nude images.”

The lawsuit included several examples of screenshots that it said would be banned under Minnesota’s law including one image shared by President Donald Trump showing him and other lawmakers floating shirtless in the Reflecting Pool at the National Mall.
The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a free speech group, said it agreed that the state law is overly broad.

“Minnesota’s law is supposed to stop AI-generated nude images, but it’s written so broadly that it could end up covering benign political memes too, like President Trump in a bikini or former President Obama in hotpants,” John Coleman, legislative council for AI and free expression at the foundation, said in a statement. “That goes far beyond prohibiting unlawful content like child sexual abuse material, which is already illegal. Instead, it sweeps in ordinary political speech and satire that Americans create and share online every day.”
“Americans have a First Amendment right to joke about, criticize, and parody public figures. A law that reaches that expression deserves to be struck down by the courts,” Coleman said.

title: Immigrant who donated lifesaving kidney to his brother is detained by ICE again
summary: José Gregorio González, who’s been his brother’s caregiver since the kidney transplant, was detained during a routine ICE check-in.
story: José Gregorio González is inside an immigration detention center almost a year after he donated his kidney to save the life of his brother, who has end-stage renal disease.
The Venezuelan man was taken into ICE custody July 21 during a routine check-in appointment with immigration authorities in Chicago.

González had been reporting to Immigration and Customs Enforcement since April on a weekly basis, sometimes more than once. The agency had placed him in an intensive supervision program to monitor his whereabouts after his yearlong humanitarian parole expired, according to his lawyer and brother.
“I don’t really see a need to necessarily detain him,” said Peter Meinecke, an attorney handling his immigration case and the managing attorney at Resurrection Project, a nonprofit group in Chicago.
“He has no criminal record and has been dutifully complying with supervision,” Meinecke told NBC News.

José Alfredo Pacheco, González’s younger brother and the recipient of his kidney, had just finished a follow-up medical appointment to monitor his recovery from the transplant he received last August. He texted González to let him know he was on his way to pick him up from his ICE check-in.
“Three minutes later, he replied, ‘Brother, I love you. They’re about to deport me.’ That was the only thing he wrote to me,” Pacheco told Noticias Telemundo in Spanish on Wednesday.
“My world came crashing down,” he said, noting that González is his sole caregiver. “My biggest fear is being left alone here.”

González’s story first made headlines in March 2025, when ICE detained him before he could donate his kidney to Pacheco. Community members in the Chicago area rallied in support of the brothers and advocated for González’s release under humanitarian parole. The brothers share the same mother.
González was temporarily released from ICE detention that April, and the brothers successfully underwent a lifesaving kidney transplant surgery in August.

“Someone who’s committed a very selfless act, like donating a kidney, is still being treated like they’re a threat to this country,” Meinecke said. “It’s an alarming precedent to be setting in terms of how we’re treating immigrants in this country.”
According to the Department of Homeland Security, González first attempted to enter the U.S. in June 2023, but Border Patrol arrested him and removed him from the country.

In December 2023, Pacheco was diagnosed with end-stage renal disease. González returned to the U.S. a month later, in January 2024, to care for his brother, who at the time needed four-hour dialysis sessions three times a week.
“In violation of our nation’s laws, he illegally re-entered the country,” a DHS spokesperson said about González’s January 2024 entry into the U.S.

González sought asylum but did not pass an initial credible fear interview, so immigration authorities placed a deportation order on him. Still, he was allowed to remain in the country under ICE supervision and with an ankle monitor to track him, which is not uncommon.
Before González’s humanitarian parole was set to expire in April, Meinecke said he filed a request to temporarily stop the government from enforcing the deportation order against his client.
That application was still pending when ICE detained González last week, Meinecke said.
According to the DHS spokesperson, González overstayed his parole in “violation of our nation’s laws.”
Meinecke said they intend to try to request another humanitarian parole for release from detention.
“While his health has more or less progressed the way you would hope following a surgery,” the attorney said about González, “his brother’s hasn’t been as straightforward.”

Pacheco said he has had two setbacks on the delicate journey to recovery from his kidney transplant. The worse one, a severe blood infection, landed him in the hospital in January. When he felt like he almost didn’t make it, Pacheco said his brother “was the only one who was with me.”

As a living organ donor, González is also under structured medical supervision to ensure his remaining kidney adapts well, Pacheco said. “He still has to attend his medical appointments, and there is no health care in Venezuela,” he said.

Venezuela’s fragile health care system had been deteriorating for years before two powerful earthquakes rattled the South American nation last month, killing more than 5,000 people and further exacerbating its ongoing health crisis.
The DHS spokesperson said González will “remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings” to Venezuela.

On Sunday, Pacheco spoke to González, who called him from an immigration detention center in Missouri, where he is being held. Pacheco said his older brother never complained about the situation and instead insisted he not worry about him.
“It’s very hard when we siblings are so close,” Pacheco said with emotion. “We would give our lives for one another. … He is the best of us all.”

title: Trump says he’ll revive ‘anti-weaponization’ fund if Blanche’s nomination for AG is blocked
summary: Trump threatened to “push hard” to keep a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund active, amid an ongoing feud between two Republican senators and the Trump administration over Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general.
story: President Donald Trump on Saturday threatened to “push hard” to keep a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund active, amid an ongoing feud between two Republican senators and the Trump administration over the president’s nomination of Todd Blanche for attorney general.

“If Senators Cornyn and Tillis, both upset because I wouldn’t Endorse them (they lost, and quit, respectively!), aren’t going to approve Todd Blanche, one of the most respected professionals, according to everybody, in the Country, to be the United States Attorney General, then I will keep Todd as Acting A.G., and push hard to get the Anti-Weaponization Bill, which takes care of those who have been so badly treated by the Crooked Joe Biden (and Obuma!) Administration (I get nothing, although I was treated horribly!), PASSED,” the president wrote in a post on Truth Social.
“Todd Blanche was a voice of reason! It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done. Thank you for your attention to this matter!” he added.

Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., are both departing Congress after feuding with Trump. In Texas, Cornyn ran for re-election, losing in a primary runoff to state Attorney General Ken Paxton after Trump endorsed Paxton.
Tillis, in North Carolina, opted not to run for re-election, making his plans to retire public one day after drawing Trump’s ire for opposing a GOP-backed domestic policy package.

The two senators have partially conditioned their support for Blanche’s nomination on the Trump administration rescinding its plans for the fund, which would provide compensation for Jan. 6 rioters pardoned by Trump for claims of government overreach.
In a post on X following Trump’s statement Saturday, Tillis blamed the president for Blanche’s stalled confirmation.

“Despite comments as late as yesterday that the fund is dead, President Trump clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against,” he wrote.
“It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal. Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday,” Tillis added.

Blanche’s nomination has been in jeopardy for several weeks, with Cornyn and Tillis previously saying that there are other Republican senators that share their concerns but don’t sit on the Judiciary Committee and wouldn’t have the chance to vote for or against Blanche until his nomination came to the floor.
On Wednesday night, the committee postponed a vote on Blanche’s nomination because of Cornyn and Tillis’ concerns.
On Friday, at a Cabinet meeting, the president defended the fund, saying, “It is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t.”
“This has nothing to do with Todd,” Trump added.
The anti-weaponization fund has been blocked indefinitely by a federal judge, but the Trump administration has not pledged to stop pursuing it.

The fund was part of a settlement agreement that stemmed from a lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS. Also part of that settlement was an agreement that made the president and several family members immune from IRS audits, another provision that Cornyn and Tillis have shared concerns about.
Earlier this week, the president threatened to withdraw Blanche’s nomination and resubmit it next year, after Tillis and Cornyn have left office.

“Hey, in 158 days they can try it again, roll the dice on what the Senate confirmation process looks like next year,” Tillis told reporters at the Capitol after that threat. “It’s all on him. Certainly within his authority to do that.”

title: Vermont’s GOP governor defends state-run elections and mail-in voting
summary: Vermont’s GOP governor, Phil Scott, defended mail-in voting and state-run elections as a good option for Americans, rejecting Trump’s calls for the Republicans to “nationalize” elections and limit options for mail-in voting.
story: Vermont’s GOP Gov. Phil Scott on Friday defended mail ballots and state-run elections, rejecting President Donald Trump’s calls for Republicans to “nationalize” elections and limit options for mail-in voting.

Asked how he responds to Trump’s call for voting to be nationalized, Scott said he goes back to the 10th Amendment, noting that it’s “clear on the role of the states in terms of elections. So I think that we should follow that and we’re closer to the people.”

“In Vermont, I would have to say, mail-in ballots are popular. Who are they popular with? Republicans,” Scott told “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker during a common ground conversation with North Carolina Democratic Gov. Josh Stein at the National Governors Association meeting in Oklahoma City.
The governor added that mail-in voting has increased voter participation among members of his party in his state, which in turn has boosted GOP representation in the state Legislature.
“We’re closer to our people and we know what’s right and what’s wrong, and we can control the elections,” Scott added, defending the role of states in administering elections.

“I would hope that all, if not the majority, of Democrats would agree that this is ours, not the federal government’s,” he said. “We were here before the federal government was, the states were, and so we formed the government. Now they’re getting bloated, and we need to protect our rights.”
Scott’s remarks come as Trump this year has continued his yearslong opposition to mail-in voting, falsely claiming that it is rife with fraud and abuse.
The claims have fueled the president’s desire to pass the SAVE America Act, a major piece of federal legislation to overhaul election administration, that has stalled in Congress.

Trump has repeatedly said that the bill would ban mail-in voting in most cases, which is not true, though the SAVE Act would impose additional requirements for citizens before registering to vote and casting a ballot.
The president himself, in a Florida special election earlier this year, voted by mail, saying it was alright for him to do so because “I’m president of the United States.”
Still, he continued to call mail-in voting “mail-in cheating” after using that method to vote.
Earlier this year, Trump also said in a podcast interview that Republicans should aim to “nationalize the voting,” comments that drew condemnation from both sides of the aisle.

White House spokeswoman Abigail Jackson on Friday responded to Scott’s remarks by saying in a statement that Trump “is committed to ensuring that Americans have full confidence in the administration of elections.” She said the president “will also continue urging Congress to pass the SAVE America Act.”

In federal courts, the Trump administration has defended an executive order the president signed that aimed to create federal lists of voters and would have required mail-in ballots to be sent only to voters on those lists. A federal judge last month blocked that order, saying it’s unconstitutional for the federal government to intervene in the administration of state elections. Trump has appealed the case to the Supreme Court, asking for permission to impose the executive order as soon as August so that it can be in effect for the upcoming midterm elections.

Scott’s comments Friday came during a moderated conversation with Stein, who said Trump’s repeated disparagement of mail-in voting and the current election system “is immensely damaging to the health of our democracy.”

The pair also spoke about a lawsuit that Vermont and North Carolina have signed onto opposing the Trump administration’s decision to condition the release of some state funds for emergency preparedness on compliance with the president’s demands for election administration reforms.

“When a disaster strikes, our objective, whether it’s local government, state government or federal government, must be to do everything in our power to save life and to help people get their lives back together,” Stein said. “So the notion that you would condition that on a state agreeing to something is offensive.”

Still, Stein said, some of the proposed reforms to the Federal Emergency Management Agency would be a “step in the right direction,” in making a process for disaster response that’s led by states and assisted by the federal government.

“When you think about something like a disaster, it should be locally driven, state managed and federally supported. And so, the resources are where it’s really critical that the federal government step up,” the North Carolina governor said.

He added later, “There’s the FEMA Review Council, and initially they were talking about eliminating FEMA altogether, and I was opposed to that. And now what they’re heading toward is much more flexibility and quicker money to states, so that we can then respond quickly, and that’s a step in the right direction.”

The two governors also spoke about the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda and called for lawmakers in Congress to pass lasting immigration reform, which Stein and Scott each said would take rising above the current political rhetoric.

“We need more immigration from my standpoint. Legal immigration. There’s got to be a pathway to do that,” Scott said, adding that it could happen if lawmakers forget about “partisanship, elections, thinking about who’s going to be in power, what can we do to leverage this to get in power.”
He added, “Forget about the next election. Just do the right thing, and nine times out of 10, that’s what works.”
Stein agreed, telling Welker, “Our immigration system does not work well. Congress refuses to act. They are too happy to score political points rather than to address a real problem.”

title: Trump appeals ruling that found his $10B IRS suit aimed to ‘manipulate’ legal proceedings
summary: The case is at the center of negotiations between two Republican senators and the Justice Department over Todd Blanche’s nomination to serve as attorney general.
story: President Donald Trump on Friday took the first step in appealing a federal judge’s ruling that questioned the legality of a lawsuit filed by the president, two of his sons and the Trump Organization against the IRS.

The Trumps filed notice that they would appeal the July 13 ruling by U.S. District Judge Kathleen Williams that said the $10 billion suit was for an “improper purpose.” The case led to the Justice Department creating a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund as part of a settlement that included an agreement that the government would not investigate or seek any sort of payment from the president, his family members and companies on pending tax claims.
The IRS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the forthcoming appeal.

A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said Friday that the IRS “wrongly allowed a rogue, politically-motivated employee to leak private and confidential information about President Trump, his family, and the Trump Organization” to news outlets that was later “illegally released to millions of people.”
A former IRS contractor pleaded guilty in 2023 to stealing Trump’s tax records and thousands of others in 2019 and 2020 before leaking them. He is serving a five-year prison term.

The president sued the IRS and the Treasury Department in January over allegations that the agency was at fault for an unauthorized release of his tax documents that led to a report in The New York Times that said Trump had paid only $750 in federal income taxes in 2016 and 2017.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google

In her ruling, Williams, a Barack Obama appointee, said Trump sued the IRS over his leaked tax records to “manipulate the judicial process” rather than to “vindicate rights.” She also pointed out that Trump has jurisdiction over the Justice Department, Treasury Department and the IRS.

The ruling said the Justice Department could not portray the settlement with Trump as a judicial agreement. The judge also ordered sanctions against acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, a former personal lawyer to Trump, and Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, in addition to asking the Florida Bar Association to consider whether disciplinary action was necessary for one of Trump’s attorneys, Alejandro Brito.
The unprecedented settlement is at the center of a standoff between two Republican senators and the Justice Department that has stalled a vote on Blanche’s nomination for attorney general.

Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., have demanded that the DOJ agree to permanently shut down the “anti-weaponization” fund and narrow the audit protection deal before they will commit to advancing Blanche’s nomination.

Trump on Friday morning acknowledged the fund is dead but told reporters, “I wish it weren’t.” He did not answer a question about whether he’d agree to limit the terms of the tax deal for himself, his family and his company.

title: DOJ drops Reflecting Pool case, blaming damage on ‘botched’ installation
summary: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration has dropped its case against a former Olympic canoeist charged in connection with damage to the Reflecting Pool, acknowledging their allegations against David “Davey” Hearn don’t hold water.
story: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration has dropped its case against a former Olympic canoeist charged in connection with damage to the Reflecting Pool, acknowledging their allegations against David “Davey” Hearn don’t hold water.

In a filing Friday afternoon, a supervisor in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, which is headed by Jeanine Pirro, wrote that officials obtained information that undermined “the evidentiary basis for the indictment” against Hearn.

Prosecutors said that after the indictment came down on July 2, the Interior Department provided additional documents to the U.S. Attorney’s Office “indicating that damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in June 2026 was the result of flawed installation by the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings.”
DOJ said it “first became aware of information showing that the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism” after reviewing more documents.
“Had [the Interior Department] been forthcoming with the information clearly in its possession, the government would not have sought a grand jury indictment,” the filing said.

DOJ said when it presented the case to a grand jury, it was “not in possession of any information from DOI indicating that any damage to the Reflecting Pool was caused by anything other than the actions of the defendant and other vandals who damaged the pool’s lining.”

The Justice Department filing said that based on its review of evidence, “it is difficult to attribute the widespread damage to the Reflecting Pool to vandalism, let alone to establish that fact beyond a reasonable doubt.”

A spokesperson for Pirro said the filing spoke for itself. Her office also moved to dismiss at least one of the other three misdemeanor cases that had been brought in connection with the Reflecting Pool.

President Donald Trump blamed vandals for the issues with the pool after he announced a plan to coat the bottom with “American flag blue” ahead of America’s 250th birthday. The project faced several setbacks, and the cost grew considerably beyond his original estimates. The coating began coming up and algae flooded the water once the pool was refilled.

Trump has made repeated claims about vandals cutting 350-foot slits into the Reflecting Pool — saying at different times they used a knife, a box cutter and a razor. He called the alleged vandals “thugs” and said they were “sick” and “terrible.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday evening.

Hearn had told NBC News that the pool’s condition was exactly the same after he stuck his hands in the water as it was when he arrived. He pleaded not guilty after he was charged with destruction of property and accused of doing more than $1,000 worth of damage to the pool.

“The Government’s case against Davey Hearn should never have been brought,” Hearn attorney Steven Levin said in a statement  Friday. “Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American. The government’s approach was ready, shoot, aim. The federal government owes Mr. Hearn an apology.”

The government’s case against Hearn had been flooded with problems. A key witness initially wasn’t able to represent to a grand jury that the damage the government accused Hearn of causing would have cost more than $1,000, the key threshold it needed to meet to bring a felony case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Kevin Reddington, a rookie federal prosecutor, earlier in the week accused Hearn’s defense attorneys of violating grand jury secrecy rules. But as Hearn’s defense attorneys noted, the rules that Reddington cited applied to government attorneys, not defense attorneys.

title: Abortion is on the ballot again in these two states: From the Politics Desk
summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Adam Edelman previews two under-the-radar ballot measures that voters will decide on in next week’s primaries. Plus, our Capitol Hill team has the latest on Todd Blanche’s confirmation saga.
Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.
— Adam Wollner
Abortion is on the ballot again in two states
Following the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision to overturn Roe v. Wade, abortion rights advocates brought the fight to the states — including red ones.

That year, Kansas voters overwhelmingly struck down a proposed constitutional amendment that would have removed language enshrining abortion rights in their state — the first victory that year in what quickly became a clean sweep in six states. Two years later, Missouri voters approved a ballot initiative that effectively protected abortion rights until fetal viability — one of seven states where similar measures passed that cycle.

Next Tuesday, abortion is on the ballot again in these two states — albeit indirectly. In Missouri, one initiative on the ballot would require citizen-led constitutional amendments to secure a majority in all eight congressional districts — a significantly higher bar than the current threshold of a simple statewide majority.

In Kansas, voters will weigh in on a proposal to change how state Supreme Court justices are chosen. Currently, the governor (who since 2019 has been a Democrat) gets to appoint justices to the bench, selected from a list created by a nine-member nonpartisan commission. Tuesday’s ballot measure would instead allow for the direct election of state Supreme Court justices. In a state where registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats 2 to 1, the proposal essentially bets that voters will reliably elect conservative — and anti-abortion — justices.

Republican legislative supermajorities in both states referred those measures to the August primary ballot — not the November general election — another bet that diminished summer voter turnout could boost their prospects of passage.

“Make no mistake about it — this is happening because the people have been winning on progressive issues,” said Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, the executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center, which works with progressive organizations to help advance citizen-led ballot measures.

In states like Kansas and Missouri that reliably elect Republicans up and down the ballot, the citizen-led ballot measure process is one of the few ways liberals have been able to score wins in recent years.
In Missouri, for example, some of the other most recent constitutional amendments passed by voters include the legalization of recreational marijuana in 2022 and Medicaid expansion in 2020.

A September analysis by Bolts magazine, which focuses on state and local politics, concluded that all five of the citizen-led ballot initiatives approved by Missouri voters since 2020 would have been rejected under the proposed threshold.

Republicans in other states are also seeking to make it more difficult for citizen-led constitutional amendments to pass. Voters in North Dakota and South Dakota will decide this fall whether to raise the requirement for passage to 60%. In Utah, voters will be asked to bump up the threshold for ballot measures specifically related to increasing taxes.
Trump defends ‘anti-weaponization’ fund, further complicating Blanche nomination

President Donald Trump defended his administration’s controversial proposal for a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund for Jan. 6 defendants and others who he says were unfairly targeted by the government.

Trump’s continued flirtation with the fund undermines assurances from his acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, and others in the administration that the idea, which faces strong opposition from some key Republicans, is dead.

It’s thrown Blanche’s nomination to be the nation’s chief law enforcement official into limbo, with two Republicans — Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — blocking it over concerns about the settlement between Trump and the IRS that created the fund.

But Trump’s comments today are only worsening tensions with the two senators. Asked at a Cabinet meeting if the fund is dead, Trump replied: “It is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t. To be honest with you, I think people were horribly treated, horribly abused. This has nothing to do with Todd.”
Blanche is now unlikely to be confirmed before the Senate departs next week for its five-week summer recess. The chamber is not slated to return until after Labor Day.

In a post on Truth Social earlier in the day, Trump specifically lashed out at Cornyn, suggesting that he was standing in the way of the Blanche nomination because Trump had endorsed the longtime senator’s primary challenger, Ken Paxton.
Cornyn has not directly responded to Trump’s post. But he reposted two individuals who questioned Trump’s comments on X.
